Module 3 · PL/SQL · 3.1d

Control Structures

Statements that control the flow of execution — making decisions and repeating tasks in PL/SQL programs.

What are Control Structures?

Control Structures are statements that control the flow of execution of a PL/SQL program. They help the program make decisions and repeat tasks.

There are two main types:

🔀

Decision Making

IF · IF-ELSE · ELSIF · CASE

🔁

Looping

LOOP · WHILE LOOP · FOR LOOP

Syntax Reference

IF Statement

PL/SQL
IF condition THEN
    -- Statements to execute if condition is true
END IF;

IF-ELSE Statement

PL/SQL
IF condition THEN
    -- Statements to execute if condition is true
ELSE
    -- Statements to execute if condition is false
END IF;

ELSIF Statement

PL/SQL
IF condition1 THEN
    -- Statements to execute if condition1 is true
ELSIF condition2 THEN
    -- Statements to execute if condition2 is true
ELSE
    -- Statements to execute if none of the conditions are true
END IF;

CASE Statement

PL/SQL
CASE expression
    WHEN value1 THEN
        -- Statements to execute if expression equals value1
    WHEN value2 THEN
        -- Statements to execute if expression equals value2
    ELSE
        -- Statements to execute if expression doesn't match any value
END CASE;

LOOP Statement

PL/SQL
LOOP
    -- Statements to execute repeatedly
    EXIT WHEN condition; -- Optional exit condition
END LOOP;

WHILE LOOP Statement

PL/SQL
WHILE condition LOOP
    -- Statements to execute repeatedly while condition is true
END LOOP;

FOR LOOP Statement

PL/SQL
FOR counter IN initial_value..final_value LOOP
    -- Statements to execute repeatedly for each value in the range
END LOOP;

Examples

1) ELSIF — Grade Checker

PL/SQL
DECLARE
   marks NUMBER := 75;
BEGIN
   -- Check first condition
   IF marks >= 90 THEN
      DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Grade A');
   -- Check second condition
   ELSIF marks >= 75 THEN
      DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Grade B');
   -- Remaining cases
   ELSE
      DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Grade C');
   END IF;
END;
/

2) CASE Statement

PL/SQL
DECLARE
   grade CHAR(1) := 'A';
BEGIN
   -- Compare grade value
   CASE
      WHEN grade = 'A' THEN
         DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Excellent');
      WHEN grade = 'B' THEN
         DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Very Good');
      ELSE
         DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Good');
   END CASE;
END;
/

3) LOOP

PL/SQL
DECLARE
   i NUMBER := 1;
BEGIN
   LOOP
      -- Print current value
      DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(i);
      -- Increase value
      i := i + 1;
      -- Exit when i becomes greater than 5
      EXIT WHEN i > 5;
   END LOOP;
END;
/

4) WHILE LOOP

PL/SQL
DECLARE
   i NUMBER := 1;
BEGIN
   WHILE i <= 5 LOOP
      -- Print current value
      DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(i);
      -- Increase value
      i := i + 1;
   END LOOP;
END;
/

5) FOR LOOP

PL/SQL
DECLARE
   i NUMBER;
BEGIN
   FOR i IN 1..5 LOOP
      -- Print current value
      DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(i);
   END LOOP;
END;
/
Module 3 · PL/SQL · 3.1e

Error Handling

Catching runtime errors gracefully — predefined exceptions, user-defined exceptions, and the RAISE keyword.

What is an Exception?

An Exception is a runtime error that occurs while executing a PL/SQL program. If an exception occurs and is not handled, the program stops immediately.

Examples:

  • Dividing a number by zero
  • Selecting data that does not exist
  • Inserting duplicate values
  • Invalid data conversion

Why Do We Need Exception Handling?

Suppose you write a banking program.

Withdraw Money
↓
Check Balance
↓
Balance Available?
↓
Yes → Withdraw  ·  No → Show Error
❌

Without Exception Handling

Program crashes. User gets an error message. Remaining statements are not executed.

✅

With Exception Handling

Error is caught. Friendly message is displayed. Program continues gracefully.

Syntax

PL/SQL — Block Structure
DECLARE
   -- Variable Declaration
BEGIN
   -- Executable Statements
EXCEPTION
   -- Error Handling
END;

Code Example

PL/SQL
DECLARE
   -- Declare two variables
   num1 NUMBER := 10;
   num2 NUMBER := 0;
   result NUMBER;
BEGIN
   -- This statement causes an exception
   result := num1 / num2;
   DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(result);
EXCEPTION
   -- Handle divide by zero error
   WHEN ZERO_DIVIDE THEN
      DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Error: Cannot divide by zero.');
END;
/
ℹ️ Output
Error: Cannot divide by zero.

Java vs PL/SQL Exception Comparison

JavaPL/SQL
tryBEGIN
catchEXCEPTION
throwRAISE
finallyNo direct equivalent
ExceptionException

Predefined Exceptions

These exceptions are already defined by Oracle. You only need to use their names.

ExceptionCause
ZERO_DIVIDEDivision by zero
NO_DATA_FOUNDSELECT returns no rows
TOO_MANY_ROWSSELECT returns more than one row
INVALID_NUMBERInvalid number conversion
VALUE_ERRORData type or size mismatch
DUP_VAL_ON_INDEXDuplicate value in a unique column
CURSOR_ALREADY_OPENCursor opened twice
LOGIN_DENIEDInvalid username/password
STORAGE_ERRORMemory allocation error

User-Defined Exceptions

Sometimes Oracle has no predefined exception for your business rule. In that case, we create our own exception.

Syntax

PL/SQL
DECLARE
   -- Declare a user-defined exception
   my_exception EXCEPTION;
BEGIN
   -- Raise the exception when a condition is met
   IF some_condition THEN
      RAISE my_exception;
   END IF;
EXCEPTION
   -- Handle the user-defined exception
   WHEN my_exception THEN
      DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('User-defined exception occurred.');
END;
/

Code

PL/SQL
DECLARE
   age NUMBER := 15;
   invalid_age EXCEPTION;
BEGIN
   IF age < 18 THEN
      RAISE invalid_age;
   END IF;
EXCEPTION
   WHEN invalid_age THEN
      DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Not Eligible');
END;
/

RAISE Keyword

  • Used to explicitly raise an exception.
  • Can raise predefined or user-defined exceptions.

Syntax

PL/SQL
RAISE exception_name;

Code

PL/SQL
IF salary < 0 THEN
   RAISE invalid_salary;
END IF;

Advantages & Disadvantages

✅

Advantages

Prevents program crashes.
Displays meaningful error messages.
Makes programs more reliable.
Easier debugging.
Improves user experience.

❌

Disadvantages

Adds extra code.
Incorrect exception handling may hide real problems.
Overusing WHEN OTHERS can make debugging difficult.

Module 3 · PL/SQL · 3.1f

Cursors

A pointer to the result set of an SQL query — allowing PL/SQL to process query results one row at a time.

What is a Cursor?

  • A Cursor is a pointer (reference) to the result set returned by an SQL query.
  • It allows PL/SQL to process query results one row at a time.
  • A Cursor is a mechanism used to retrieve and process rows returned by an SQL query one by one.

Why Do We Need Cursors?

Suppose the Employee table contains:

Emp_IDNameSalary
101Vishal50000
102Rahul60000
103Aman55000

Query: SELECT * FROM Employee; — This query returns 3 rows.

Question: How will PL/SQL process each row individually? Answer: Using a Cursor.

Without a cursor: You cannot process multiple rows one by one. Business logic becomes difficult.

Types of Cursors

1. Implicit Cursors 2. Explicit Cursors

1. Implicit Cursors

  • Automatically created by Oracle for all SQL statements.
  • No need to declare or manage them manually.
  • Examples: SELECT INTO, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
PL/SQL — Implicit Cursor
DECLARE
   emp_name VARCHAR2(20);
BEGIN
   -- Oracle automatically creates an implicit cursor
   SELECT name
   INTO emp_name
   FROM Employee
   WHERE emp_id = 101;
   DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(emp_name);
END;
/

2. Explicit Cursors

  • Declared and managed by the programmer.
  • Used when you need more control over processing rows.

Steps:

a
Declare the cursor
↓
b
Open the cursor
↓
c
Fetch data from the cursor
↓
d
Close the cursor
PL/SQL — Explicit Cursor Example
DECLARE
    CURSOR emp_cursor IS
        SELECT emp_id, emp_name FROM employees;
    emp_record emp_cursor%ROWTYPE;
BEGIN
    OPEN emp_cursor;
    LOOP
        FETCH emp_cursor INTO emp_record;
        EXIT WHEN emp_cursor%NOTFOUND;
        DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(emp_record.emp_name);
    END LOOP;
    CLOSE emp_cursor;
END;

Cursor Operations

OperationDescriptionSyntax
OPENInitializes the cursor and executes the SQL query.OPEN cursor_name;
FETCHRetrieves the next row from the cursor into variables.FETCH cursor_name INTO variable1, variable2, ...;
CLOSECloses the cursor and releases the resources.CLOSE cursor_name;

Cursor Attributes

%ISOPEN — Checks if the cursor is open %FOUND — Returns TRUE if last FETCH found a row %NOTFOUND — Returns TRUE if last FETCH found no row %ROWCOUNT — Returns number of rows processed so far

Complete Code

PL/SQL
DECLARE
   -- Variable to store employee name
   emp_name VARCHAR2(20);
   -- Declare an explicit cursor
   CURSOR emp_cursor IS
      SELECT name FROM Employee;
BEGIN
   -- Execute the query
   OPEN emp_cursor;
   -- Fetch first row into variable
   FETCH emp_cursor INTO emp_name;
   -- Print fetched value
   DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(emp_name);
   -- Release cursor resources
   CLOSE emp_cursor;
END;
/

Advantages & Disadvantages

✅

Advantages

Processes multiple rows one by one.
Improves control over query results.
Useful for complex business logic.
Supports row-by-row processing.
Makes data processing flexible.

❌

Disadvantages

Slower than set-based SQL operations.
Consumes memory.
Requires manual management (OPEN, FETCH, CLOSE).
Incorrect handling may cause resource leaks.

Module 3 · PL/SQL · 3.1g

Procedures and Functions

Named, reusable PL/SQL blocks stored permanently in the Oracle database — the difference between doing something and returning something.

What is a Procedure?

  • A Procedure is a named PL/SQL block that performs a specific task.
  • It is stored permanently in the Oracle database and can be called whenever needed.
  • A Procedure is a reusable program used to perform one or more operations.

Syntax

PL/SQL
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE procedure_name IS
BEGIN
   -- Executable Statements
END;
/

What is a Function?

  • A Function is also a named PL/SQL block, but it must return exactly one value using the RETURN statement.
  • A Function is a reusable program that performs a task and always returns a value.

Syntax

PL/SQL
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION function_name RETURN data_type IS
BEGIN
   -- Executable Statements
   RETURN value;
END;
/

Why Do We Need Procedures and Functions?

  • To avoid code duplication.
  • To improve code organization and readability.
  • To enhance maintainability of the code.
  • To allow for modular programming.

Examples

1) Procedure Example — greet

PL/SQL
-- Create a procedure
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE greet
IS
BEGIN
   -- Print greeting message
   DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Welcome to PL/SQL');
END;
/
-- Execute the procedure
BEGIN
   greet;
END;
/

2) Function Example — add_numbers

PL/SQL
-- Create a function
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION add_numbers(a NUMBER, b NUMBER) RETURN NUMBER
IS
BEGIN
   -- Return the sum of a and b
   RETURN a + b;
END;
/
-- Execute the function
DECLARE
   result NUMBER;
BEGIN
   result := add_numbers(10, 20);
   DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Sum: ' || result);
END;
/

Parameters in PL/SQL

🔖 a) IN Parameter
Used to pass values to the procedure or function. The value of an IN parameter cannot be changed inside the procedure or function. Data goes from the calling environment to the procedure/function.
PL/SQL
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE greet_user(name IN VARCHAR2)
IS
BEGIN
   DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Hello, ' || name);
END;
/
-- Execute the procedure
BEGIN
   greet_user('Vishal');
END;
/
✅ b) OUT Parameter
Used to return values from the procedure to the calling environment. Data goes from the procedure/function to the calling environment.
PL/SQL
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE get_user_info(user_id IN NUMBER, user_name OUT VARCHAR2)
IS
BEGIN
   SELECT name INTO user_name FROM users WHERE id = user_id;
END;
/
-- Execute the procedure
BEGIN
   get_user_info(1, :user_name);
END;
/
ℹ️ c) IN OUT Parameter
Used to pass values to the procedure and return modified values back to the calling environment. Data goes both ways between the calling environment and the procedure/function.
PL/SQL
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE update_salary(emp_id IN NUMBER, salary IN OUT NUMBER)
IS
BEGIN
   UPDATE employees SET salary = salary + 1000 WHERE id = emp_id;
   SELECT salary INTO salary FROM employees WHERE id = emp_id;
END;
/
-- Execute the procedure
DECLARE
   emp_salary NUMBER := 50000;
BEGIN
   update_salary(1, emp_salary);
   DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Updated Salary: ' || emp_salary);
END;
/

Advantages & Disadvantages

✅

Advantages

Code Reusability
Modular Programming
Easy Maintenance
Better Performance (stored in database)
Improved Security
Reduces Duplicate Code

❌

Disadvantages

More difficult to debug than simple SQL.
Requires database privileges.
Too many procedures/functions can make maintenance harder if poorly organized.

Module 3 · PL/SQL · 3.1h

Packages

A collection of related PL/SQL objects — procedures, functions, variables, and more — stored together under a single name.

What is a Package?

  • A Package is a collection (group) of related PL/SQL objects stored together under a single name.
  • A package can contain: Procedures · Functions · Variables · Constants · Cursors · Exceptions
ℹ️ Simple Definition
A Package is a container that groups related PL/SQL procedures, functions, variables, and other objects into one unit.

Why Do We Need Packages?

  • To organize and manage related PL/SQL code.
  • To promote code reusability and modularity.
  • To improve performance by loading related code together.
  • To enhance security by controlling access to package components.

Without Packages — Banking System

Problem — Scattered Procedures
deposit()
withdraw()
checkBalance()
transferMoney()
calculateInterest()

All procedures exist separately.
Problems:
    Difficult to manage.
    Difficult to find related code.
    Poor organization.

Solution — One Package

Organized with Package
Bank Package
│
├── deposit()
├── withdraw()
├── transferMoney()
├── checkBalance()
└── calculateInterest()

Everything related to banking is stored together.

Syntax

Package Specification

PL/SQL
CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE package_name
IS
   -- Variable Declaration
   -- Procedure Declaration
   -- Function Declaration
END package_name;
/

Package Body

PL/SQL
CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY package_name
IS
   -- Procedure Implementation
   -- Function Implementation
END package_name;
/

Example — Bank Package

Package Specification

PL/SQL
CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE bank_package
IS
   PROCEDURE deposit(amount NUMBER);
   PROCEDURE withdraw(amount NUMBER);
   FUNCTION checkBalance RETURN NUMBER;
END bank_package;
/

Package Body

PL/SQL
CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY bank_package
IS
   PROCEDURE deposit(amount NUMBER)
   IS
   BEGIN
      -- Deposit logic here
   END;

   PROCEDURE withdraw(amount NUMBER)
   IS
   BEGIN
      -- Withdraw logic here
   END;

   FUNCTION checkBalance RETURN NUMBER
   IS
      balance NUMBER;
   BEGIN
      -- Check balance logic here
      RETURN balance;
   END;
END bank_package;
/

Calling a Package Function

PL/SQL
DECLARE
   current_balance NUMBER;
BEGIN
   -- Call the checkBalance function from the bank_package
   current_balance := bank_package.checkBalance;
   DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Current Balance: ' || current_balance);
END;
/

Package Specification vs Package Body

Package SpecificationPackage Body
Contains declarationsContains implementations
Visible to usersHidden from users
Acts like an interfaceActs like the actual code
MandatoryOptional (only if implementation exists)

Advantages & Disadvantages

✅

Advantages

Groups related procedures and functions.
Improves code organization.
Supports code reusability.
Better security.
Faster execution (package is loaded once into memory).
Easier maintenance.
Supports information hiding.

❌

Disadvantages

Large packages become difficult to maintain.
Changes may require recompilation.
Beginners may find package structure confusing.

Module 3 · PL/SQL · 3.1i

Triggers

A stored PL/SQL program that automatically executes when a specific database event occurs — BEFORE, AFTER, or INSTEAD OF INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE.

What is a Trigger?

  • A Trigger is a stored PL/SQL program that is automatically executed when a specific event occurs on a database table or view.
  • A Trigger is a PL/SQL block that runs automatically in response to database events like INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE.

Why Do We Need Triggers?

Suppose an Employee table stores employee details. Whenever a new employee is added, you also want to: Save the action in a log table · Record the date and time · Record who inserted the data.

❌

Without a Trigger

INSERT Employee → Write Another SQL → Insert into Log Table. The programmer must remember to write both queries.

✅

With a Trigger

INSERT Employee → Trigger Executes Automatically → Log Table Updated. No extra SQL is required.

Trigger Execution Flow

INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE
↓
Trigger Fires
↓
Execute PL/SQL Code
↓
Complete Operation

Syntax of a Trigger

PL/SQL
CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER trigger_name
BEFORE | AFTER | INSTEAD OF
INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE
ON table_name
BEGIN
    -- Trigger Code
END;
/

Types of Triggers

🔖 1. BEFORE Trigger
Executes before the triggering event. Used for: Validation · Data checking · Preventing invalid data.
PL/SQL — Example
CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER check_salary
BEFORE INSERT
ON Employee
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
   -- Validate salary
   IF :NEW.salary < 0 THEN
      RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20001,
      'Salary cannot be negative');
   END IF;
END;
/
✅ 2. AFTER Trigger
Executes after the triggering event. Used for: Logging · Auditing · Updating related tables.
PL/SQL — Example
CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER log_employee_insert
AFTER INSERT
ON Employee
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
   INSERT INTO Employee_Log(emp_id, action_date)
   VALUES(:NEW.emp_id, SYSDATE);
END;
ℹ️ 3. INSTEAD OF Trigger
Used for views — executes instead of the triggering event. Allows custom logic when inserting/updating/deleting from a view.
PL/SQL — Example
CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER employee_view_trigger
INSTEAD OF INSERT
ON Employee_View
BEGIN
   INSERT INTO Employee(name, salary)
   VALUES(:NEW.name, :NEW.salary);
END;

Special Variables in Triggers

VariableDescription
:NEWRefers to the new values being inserted or updated in the table.
:OLDRefers to the old values being updated or deleted from the table.

Advantages & Disadvantages

✅

Advantages

Executes automatically.
Enforces business rules.
Maintains data integrity.
Useful for auditing and logging.
Reduces duplicate code.

❌

Disadvantages

Difficult to debug.
Hidden execution may confuse developers.
Too many triggers can reduce performance.
Multiple triggers on the same table may become difficult to manage.

Module 5 · Spring Core & Maven · 5a

Introduction to Spring Framework

An open-source Java framework that helps developers build applications more easily, quickly, and efficiently — the ready-made construction kit for Java.

What is Spring Framework?

  • Spring Framework is an open-source Java framework that helps developers build Java applications more easily, quickly, and efficiently.
  • It provides many pre-built features so that developers don't have to write everything from scratch.
House Building Analogy
Imagine you have to build a house. You can either buy every brick, cement, and tool separately and build everything yourself — OR use a ready-made construction kit that already contains everything you need.

Spring Framework is like that ready-made construction kit for Java developers. Instead of writing thousands of lines of repetitive code, Spring provides them for you.

What is a Framework?

Before understanding Spring, you must know what a framework is.

A Framework is a collection of pre-written code, libraries, and rules that helps developers build applications faster. It provides a structure for your project.

❌

Without Framework

Developer writes everything manually — from scratch, every single time.

✅

With Framework

Developer → Spring Framework → Provides ready-made features.

Why Do We Need Spring Framework?

Before Spring existed, developers mainly used Java EE to build enterprise applications.

Problem 1: Too Much Boilerplate Code

Developers had to write a lot of repetitive code. Example:

  • Database connection
  • Object creation
  • Exception handling
  • Transaction management

Even simple applications became very lengthy.

Problem 2: Tight Coupling

Classes directly created other objects.

Java — Tight Coupling
Car car = new Car();
Engine engine = new Engine();

Every class became dependent on another class. Changing one class often required changes in many other classes. We'll understand this deeply in the Dependency Injection topic.

Problem 3: Difficult Testing

Since objects were created manually, writing unit tests became difficult.

Problem 4: Difficult Maintenance

Large projects contained thousands of classes. Managing everything manually became complicated.

Problem 5: Poor Reusability

Code was tightly connected, making it difficult to reuse.

Spring Solves These Problems

Traditional JavaSpring Framework
More codingLess coding
Manual object creationAutomatic object management
Difficult testingEasy testing
Tightly coupled codeLoosely coupled code
Hard maintenanceEasy maintenance
💡 Conclusion
Spring Framework is a powerful tool that simplifies Java development. It reduces boilerplate code, promotes loose coupling, and makes testing and maintenance easier.

Example: Restaurant Analogy

😤

Without Spring

You must: Cook the food · Arrange utensils · Wash dishes · Serve yourself. Everything is your responsibility.

😊

With Spring

You simply order food. The restaurant: Prepares food · Serves food · Cleans dishes · Manages everything. You only enjoy the meal.

Spring works in a similar way — it handles much of the application's infrastructure so you can focus on writing business logic.

Spring Modules (Overview)

  • Spring is not a single library. It is a framework made up of many independent modules.
  • It consists of many modules.
Toolbox Analogy 🧰
A toolbox is not just one tool. It contains a screwdriver, hammer, wrench, pliers, etc. You use only the tools you need.

Similarly, Spring contains many modules. You include only the modules required for your project.

Why are there different modules?

Imagine you are building different types of applications.

  • A Console Application doesn't need web features.
  • A Web Application needs MVC.
  • A Banking Application needs database support.
  • A Large Enterprise Application needs security, transactions, logging, etc.

Instead of putting everything into one huge library, Spring divides features into modules.

ModulePurpose
CoreCore features of Spring
IoCManages object creation (covered later)
AOPHandles cross-cutting concerns like logging
Data AccessSimplifies database operations
ORMIntegrates with Hibernate and other ORM tools
MVCBuild web applications
BootQuickly create Spring applications

Benefits of Using Spring

Reduces code Easy to maintain Easy to test Modular architecture Supports enterprise applications Integrates with many technologies Improves developer productivity
Module 5 · Spring Core & Maven · 5b · i

Introduction to Maven Build Tool

Maven — the project manager for Java that automates compiling, dependency management, testing, and packaging so you can focus on writing code.

What is a Build?

A build is a process of converting source code into a standalone form that can be run on a computer. It typically involves compiling the code, packaging it into an executable format, and sometimes running tests to ensure the code works as expected.

What is a Build Tool?

A build tool is a software application that automates the process of building software. It helps developers manage dependencies, compile code, run tests, and package the application for deployment. Build tools can also provide features like versioning, continuous integration, and deployment automation.

What is Maven?

  • Maven is a popular build automation tool used primarily for Java projects.
  • It simplifies the build process by providing a standard way to manage project dependencies, compile code, run tests, and package applications.
  • Maven uses a Project Object Model (POM) file to define the project's structure, dependencies, and build configuration.
Project Manager Analogy
Think of Maven as a Project Manager. You tell Maven: "I want to build my project." Maven replies: "Don't worry! I'll compile your code, download required libraries, run tests, package your application, and prepare it for deployment."

Why Do We Need Maven?

Before Maven existed, Java development involved many manual tasks. Let's understand the problems.

Problem 1: Manual Library Management

Suppose you want to use the Spring Framework.

⚠️ Without Maven
Search for the Spring JAR files online → Download each JAR manually → Copy them into your project → Repeat this for every library.

Now imagine your project requires 50 libraries. This becomes tedious and error-prone.

Problem 2: Dependency Conflicts

Sometimes one library requires another library.

Dependency Tree
Spring
   │
   ├── Library A
   ├── Library B
   └── Library C

Without Maven, you would have to identify and download all of these manually. Maven resolves these transitive dependencies automatically.

Problem 3: Manual Build Process

Developers had to manually: Compile code · Run tests · Create JAR files. Doing these tasks manually for every project wastes time.

Problem 4: Different Project Structures

Every developer organized projects differently.

No Standard — Before Maven
Developer A:
    Java Files
    Images
    XML

Another Developer:
    Source
    Classes
    Resources

No standard structure existed. Maven introduced a standard directory structure that all Java developers follow.

Why Companies Use Maven

Companies use Maven because it:

Saves development time Reduces manual work Keeps projects organized Makes teamwork easier Ensures everyone uses the same library versions

How Maven Works

Step 1
Developer creates a Maven project.
↓
Step 2
Developer specifies required libraries.
↓
Step 3
Maven checks the pom.xml file.
↓
Step 4
Maven downloads missing libraries from a repository.
↓
Step 5
Maven compiles the Java code.
↓
Step 6
Maven runs tests.
↓
Step 7
Maven packages the application into a JAR or WAR file.

Diagram

Maven Flow Diagram
                    Developer
                        │
                        │
              Creates Maven Project
                        │
                        ▼
                   pom.xml File
                        │
                        ▼
                     Maven
             ┌────────┼────────┐
             │        │        │
             ▼        ▼        ▼
     Download   Compile   Run Tests
    Libraries     Code
             │
             ▼
        Package Project
             │
             ▼
       Runnable Application

Real-Life Analogy — College Fest

Event Manager Analogy
Imagine you're organizing a college fest. Without a coordinator, you have to: Book the venue · Arrange food · Invite guests · Handle decorations · Manage the budget. Doing everything yourself is difficult.

Now imagine you hire an event manager. You simply tell them: "Organize the fest." The event manager takes care of everything.

Maven is like that event manager. You focus on writing code, while Maven handles the project-building tasks.

Maven Commands

mvn — This is the command-line interface for Maven. You can use it to run various Maven commands, such as compile, package, test, and more. The mvn command reads the pom.xml file to understand the project's structure and dependencies.

🔖 1) mvn compile
This command tells Maven to compile the Java source code into class files. It looks at the pom.xml file to know what to compile and where to put the compiled files.
Terminal
mvn compile
✅ 2) mvn package
This command tells Maven to package the compiled code into a distributable format, like a JAR or WAR file. It uses the information in the pom.xml file to determine how to package the application.
Terminal
mvn package

Advantages

Automates repetitive build tasks Downloads dependencies automatically Provides a standard project structure Makes collaboration easier Simplifies version management Integrates well with IDEs and CI/CD tools
Module 5 · Spring Core & Maven · 5b · ii

Creating a New Maven Project

Setting up a standard Java project managed by Maven — from Eclipse IDE setup to the standard directory structure and pom.xml configuration.

What is a Maven Project?

A Maven Project is simply a Java project that uses Maven to:

  • Build the project
  • Manage dependencies
  • Maintain a standard folder structure
  • Package the application
ℹ️ Formula
Maven Project = Java Project + Maven

Without Maven vs With Maven

Suppose you want to build a Spring application. You have two choices:

❌

Without Maven

Create folders manually
Download libraries manually
Manage versions manually
Compile manually
Lots of manual work.

✅

With Maven

Create Maven Project
↓

Example — Project Details

FieldExamplePurpose
NameSpringDemoProject name
LocationD:\ProjectsWhere the project will be stored
JDKJava 17Java version used

Standard Directory Structure

Maven Project Structure
SpringDemo
│
├── src
│   │
│   ├── main
│   │     │

│   │     │      └── Java Source Code ( Contains all Java source files )
│   │     │

pom.xml File — The Heart of the Maven Project

  • Contains project configuration
  • Lists dependencies

Example

pom.xml

Module 5 · Spring Core & Maven · 5b · iii

Adding Spring Dependencies in pom.xml

Telling Maven exactly which libraries your project needs — understanding every tag in the dependency declaration.

What is a Dependency?

A dependency is an external library or framework that your project requires to perform certain tasks.

What is pom.xml?

The pom.xml file is the heart of every Maven project. It tells Maven:

  • Which libraries are needed.
  • Which version of each library to use.
  • How to build the project.
ℹ️ Think of it as
The instruction file for Maven.

Where Do We Add Dependencies?

Inside the <dependencies> tag.

pom.xml
<dependencies>

</dependencies>

This section contains all the libraries your project requires.

Adding the Spring Dependency

pom.xml
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        <version>6.1.10</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Understanding Every Tag

🔖 1) <dependencies>
Contains all dependencies used by the project.
pom.xml
<dependencies>
    Spring
    JUnit
    MySQL Driver
</dependencies>
🔖 2) <dependency>
Represents a single library.
pom.xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
    <version>6.1.10</version>
</dependency>
It means we are adding the "spring-context" library to our project.
ℹ️ 3) <groupId>
Represents the organization or group that created the library.
pom.xml
<groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
It means the Spring Framework is developed by the organization "org.springframework".
ℹ️ 4) <artifactId>
Represents the specific library or module you want to use.
pom.xml
<artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
It means we want to use the "spring-context" module of the Spring Framework.

Spring has many libraries:
spring-core spring-context spring-web spring-beans
ℹ️ 5) <version>
Represents the specific version of the library you want to use.
pom.xml
<version>6.1.10</version>
It means we want to use version 6.1.10 of the "spring-context" library.

What Happens After Saving?

Save pom.xml
↓
Maven Reads File
↓
Checks Local Repository
↓
If Missing
↓
Downloads Library
↓
Adds Library to Project

This usually happens automatically in IDEs like IntelliJ IDEA and Eclipse.

Full Example

pom.xml — Complete
<project>
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    <groupId>com.cognizant</groupId>
    <artifactId>SpringDemo</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>

    <!-- List of all required libraries -->
    <dependencies>
        <!-- Spring Context Library -->
        <dependency>
            <!-- Organization -->
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <!-- Library Name -->
            <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
            <!-- Version -->
            <version>6.1.10</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</project>

Advantages

Automatic library download Easy version management No manual JAR copying Faster project setup Better dependency management

Configuring Maven for Building & Managing Dependencies

Teaching Maven which Java version to use, which libraries to download, and exactly how to build and package your application — all inside pom.xml.

What Does "Configuring Maven" Mean?

Configuring Maven means telling Maven:

  • Which libraries (dependencies) the project needs.
  • Which Java version to use.
  • How to build the project.
  • How to package the application.
ℹ️ Where?
This information is written inside the pom.xml file.

Configuring Java Version

Suppose your project uses Java 17. Inside pom.xml:

pom.xml
<properties>
    <maven.compiler.source>17</maven.compiler.source>
    <maven.compiler.target>17</maven.compiler.target>
</properties>

What Do These Tags Mean?

TagPurpose
maven.compiler.source Java version used to write the code
maven.compiler.target Java version for the compiled bytecode
💡 What This Tells Maven
"Compile this project using Java 17."

Configuring Dependencies

We've already learned this. Example:

pom.xml
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        <version>6.1.10</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
💡 What This Tells Maven
"Download the Spring Context library."
Module 5 · Spring Core & Maven · 5c · i

Understanding the IoC Container

Who creates the objects? Who manages them? Understanding Control, Inversion, and the Spring IoC Container — the heart of the Spring Framework.

What Does "Control" Mean?

This is where many beginners get confused. In Spring, Control simply means: Who is responsible for creating and managing objects?

👨‍💻

Without Spring

Developer → Creates Objects

The developer has the control.

What is Inversion?

The word Inversion means: Reverse

Concept
Normally : A → B
After inversion : B → A

What is Inversion of Control (IoC)?

  • Control = Responsibility
  • Inversion = Reversed
  • Inversion of Control (IoC) means: The control of creating and managing objects is reversed.
  • In Spring, the control of creating and managing objects is given to the Spring Framework.
  • The responsibility of creating and managing objects is transferred from the programmer to the Spring Framework.

Without Spring vs With Spring

❌

Without Spring

Developer → Creates Objects

The developer has the control.

✅

With Spring

Programmer → Writes Classes → Spring → Creates Objects

Spring has the control.

What is a Container?

  • A Container is a place where objects are stored and managed.
  • In Spring, the Container is responsible for creating, managing, and destroying objects.
ℹ️ Simple Definition
Spring Container = Manager of Objects

What is the IoC Container?

The Spring IoC Container is responsible for:

Creating objects Managing objects Providing objects Destroying objects when needed
Diagram
Developer
      │
Writes Classes
      │
      ▼
+----------------------+
| Spring IoC Container |
|                      |
| Creates Objects      |
| Stores Objects       |
| Manages Objects      |
+----------------------+
         │
         ▼
     Application

Real-Life Analogy — HR Department

Without Spring
Imagine you own a company. Every employee comes to you and says: "Hire me." You personally: Hire everyone · Assign work · Manage everyone. Very difficult.
With Spring (IoC Container)
Now imagine an HR Department. Employees report to HR. HR: Hires employees · Manages employees · Assigns employees.

You simply ask HR: "I need a Java Developer." HR provides one.

Mapping

Real LifeSpring
HR DepartmentIoC Container
EmployeeObject (Bean)
Company OwnerDeveloper

Advantages

Automatic object creation Easier maintenance Reduced boilerplate code Better scalability Promotes loose coupling Simplifies testing
Module 5 · Spring IoC Container · 5c · ii

Configuring the Spring IoC Container using XML

Writing instructions in an XML file to tell Spring which objects to create, which classes they belong to, and how they are configured.

What is XML?

XML (eXtensible Markup Language) is a markup language used to store and organize data.

Unlike Java, XML does not contain business logic. It only contains configuration.

Think of XML as an instruction sheet
Teacher → Class Monitor → "Take attendance."

The teacher is not doing the work. The teacher is giving instructions.

Similarly, the XML file doesn't create objects itself. It tells Spring: "Create this object."

What is XML Configuration?

XML Configuration means writing instructions in an XML file to tell Spring:

  • Which objects (Beans) to create.
  • Which classes those objects belong to.
  • How those objects are related.

Why Do We Need XML Configuration?

Before Spring introduced annotations like @Component and @Configuration, the main way to configure Spring was XML.

Instead of writing Java code like: new Student(); — developers wrote configuration in XML. Spring would then create the object automatically.

Furniture Order Analogy
Imagine you're ordering furniture. You don't build the furniture yourself. You fill out an order form: Chair · Table · Bed. The furniture company reads the form and delivers the items.

Similarly:
Java Classes = Furniture  |  beans.xml = Order Form  |  Spring = Furniture Company

What is beans.xml?

It is the configuration file used by Spring.

Project Structure
Project
│
├── src
│
├── main
│
├── resources
│      │
│      └── beans.xml

Usually, it is stored inside: src/main/resources because Spring automatically searches for configuration files there.

Structure of beans.xml

beans.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> // XML Declaration
// version="1.0" -> Specifies the version of XML being used.
// encoding="UTF-8" -> Specifies the character encoding used in the XML file.
<beans>
    //This is the root element.
    //Every Bean must be written inside this tag.
    //Think of it as a container for all Bean definitions.
</beans>

The <bean> Tag

Suppose we have a Java class named Student.java.

Java
public class Student {

}

We want Spring to create an object of this class.

beans.xml
<bean id="student" class="com.example.Student">
    // id="student" -> This is the unique name of the bean.
    //                 It is used to reference the bean in the Spring container.
    // class="com.example.Student" -> This specifies the fully qualified name
    //                                of the Java class for which we want to create a bean.

Complete XML Example

Java Class

Java — Student.java
public class Student {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    // Getters and Setters
    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public void setName(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

    public void setAge(int age) {
        this.age = age;
    }
}

beans.xml

beans.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans>
    <bean id="student" class="com.example.Student">
        <property name="name" value="John Doe"/>
        <property name="age" value="20"/>
    </bean>
</beans>
ℹ️ What Spring Does at Startup
Spring reads the beans.xml file and creates the Student object with the specified properties. Internally it behaves like:
Java — Equivalent Code
Student student = new Student();
student.setName("John Doe");
student.setAge(20);

Advantages

  • Centralized configuration.
  • No need to write new repeatedly.
  • Easy to modify configuration without changing Java code.
  • Suitable for large enterprise applications (especially older Spring projects).
Module 5 · Spring IoC Container · 5c · iii

Defining Beans and their Dependencies

What makes a Java object a Spring Bean, how to define multiple beans in XML, and how to express dependencies between them.

What is a Bean?

  • A Bean is an object that is managed by the Spring IoC Container.
  • In Spring, a Bean is simply a Java object that is instantiated, assembled, and managed by the Spring IoC Container.
❌

Just a Java Class

public class Student { }

Is it a Bean? No. It is just a Java class.

✅

A Spring Bean

When Spring creates its object — instead of you — it becomes a Spring Bean.

Why Do We Need Beans?

Imagine a project with 500 classes.

Without Spring

Java — Manual Object Creation
new Student();
new Teacher();
new Library();
new Book();
new Employee();
new Customer();

You manually create every object. This leads to:

More code Difficult maintenance Tight coupling

With Spring

Spring creates objects for you. You simply ask Spring for the object.

Developer — Writes Classes
↓
Spring IoC Container — Creates Beans
↓
Provides Beans

You simply ask Spring for the required Bean.

Defining a Bean in XML

Java Classes

Java
public class Engine {

}
public class Car {

}

XML

beans.xml
<beans>
    <bean
        id="engine"
        class="com.demo.Engine"/>
    <bean
        id="car"
        class="com.demo.Car"/>
</beans>
ℹ️ Spring Creates
Java — Equivalent
Engine engine = new Engine();
Car car = new Car();

Understanding Dependencies

Java
class Car {
    Engine engine;
}
💡 Key Insight
Question: What does Car need?
Answer: Engine — So, Engine is Car's dependency.

Later, Spring will automatically provide the Engine Bean to the Car Bean.

Advantages

Centralized object management Reduced manual object creation Easier maintenance Better scalability Promotes loose coupling
Module 5 · Spring IoC Container · 5c · iv

ApplicationContext

The central interface for accessing the Spring IoC Container — the advanced, feature-rich implementation that powers enterprise applications.

Two Implementations of the Spring IoC Container

Spring provides two ways to use the IoC Container:

🏗️

1. BeanFactory

Basic container. Creates beans only when requested (lazy loading). Used for simple, lightweight applications.

🏭

2. ApplicationContext

Advanced container. Extends BeanFactory. Loads all beans at startup (eager loading). Used for enterprise applications.

FeatureBeanFactoryApplicationContext
Bean LoadingLazy (on demand)Eager (at startup)
Internationalization❌ No✅ Yes
Event Publishing❌ No✅ Yes
AOP SupportLimitedFull
Use CaseSimple appsEnterprise apps

What is ApplicationContext?

  • ApplicationContext is the central interface for accessing the Spring IoC Container.
  • It extends BeanFactory and provides more advanced features.
  • It is the most commonly used Spring Container.
Bank Analogy
Imagine you go to a bank.

BeanFactory = Basic ATM — Only gives cash when you ask.

ApplicationContext = Full Bank Branch — Cash, loans, insurance, fixed deposits, currency exchange — everything available.

Why Use ApplicationContext?

  • It creates all beans at startup, so they're ready to use immediately.
  • It supports internationalization (i18n).
  • It supports AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming).
  • It supports event publishing.
  • It is the standard for all enterprise-grade Spring applications.

Common Implementations of ApplicationContext

ClassUse Case
ClassPathXmlApplicationContext Loads XML configuration from the classpath (src/main/resources)
FileSystemXmlApplicationContext Loads XML configuration from the file system
AnnotationConfigApplicationContext Loads configuration from Java annotations (modern approach)

The getBean() Method

Once the ApplicationContext is created, you can retrieve beans using getBean().

Syntax

Java
ApplicationContext context =
    new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("beans.xml");
Student student = (Student) context.getBean("student");
ℹ️ What Happens Step by Step
  1. ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("beans.xml") — Spring reads the beans.xml file.
  2. Spring creates all the beans defined in beans.xml.
  3. getBean("student") — Retrieves the Student bean by its ID.
  4. The bean is returned and assigned to the variable.

Complete Example

Student.java

Java
public class Student {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    public String getName()  { return name; }
    public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public int getAge()   { return age; }
    public void setAge(int age)   { this.age = age; }
}

beans.xml

beans.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans>
    <bean id="student" class="com.example.Student">
        <property name="name" value="Vishal"/>
        <property name="age"  value="20"/>
    </bean>
</beans>

Main.java

Java
import org.springframework.context.ApplicationContext;
import org.springframework.context.support.ClassPathXmlApplicationContext;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // Step 1: Load beans.xml and create IoC Container
        ApplicationContext context =
            new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("beans.xml");

        // Step 2: Get the Student bean from the container
        Student student = (Student) context.getBean("student");

        // Step 3: Use the bean
        System.out.println("Name : " + student.getName());
        System.out.println("Age  : " + student.getAge());
    }
}
ℹ️ Output
Name : Vishal
Age : 20

Advantages

No manual object creation Advanced features (AOP, i18n, events) Standard for all enterprise Spring apps Easy to switch implementations All beans ready at startup
Module 5 · Spring IoC Container · 5c · v

BeanFactory

The simplest Spring IoC container — creates beans on demand using lazy loading, ideal for lightweight and resource-constrained applications.

What is BeanFactory?

  • BeanFactory is the simplest Spring IoC Container.
  • It creates and manages beans.
  • It creates beans only when they are requested (Lazy Loading).
ℹ️ Simple Definition
BeanFactory = Basic IoC Container = Lazy Loading

What is Lazy Loading?

Lazy Loading means: Objects are created only when they are requested, not at startup.

Pizza Shop Analogy
Eager Loading (ApplicationContext):
The pizza shop prepares all pizzas in advance. When you order, the pizza is immediately ready.

Lazy Loading (BeanFactory):
The pizza shop prepares a pizza only after you order it. It starts cooking when you place the order.
✅

Advantage of Lazy Loading

Saves memory — beans that are never requested are never created.

❌

Disadvantage of Lazy Loading

First request is slightly slower — bean creation happens on demand.

BeanFactory — Code

Student.java

Java
public class Student {
    private String name;

    public String getName() { return name; }
    public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; }
}

beans.xml

beans.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans>
    <bean id="student" class="com.example.Student">
        <property name="name" value="Vishal"/>
    </bean>
</beans>

Main.java

Java
import org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanFactory;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.xml.XmlBeanFactory;
import org.springframework.core.io.ClassPathResource;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // Step 1: Load beans.xml using BeanFactory
        BeanFactory factory =
            new XmlBeanFactory(new ClassPathResource("beans.xml"));

        // Step 2: Get the Student bean (created HERE, not at startup)
        Student student = (Student) factory.getBean("student");

        // Step 3: Use the bean
        System.out.println("Name: " + student.getName());
    }
}
ℹ️ Output
Name: Vishal

BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext

FeatureBeanFactoryApplicationContext
Bean LoadingLazy (on demand)Eager (at startup)
Memory UsageLess (beans created only when needed)More (all beans created at startup)
Performance on First CallSlower (bean created on demand)Faster (bean already available)
Internationalization❌ Not supported✅ Supported
AOP SupportLimitedFull
Event Publishing❌ Not supported✅ Supported
Use CaseSmall, simple applicationsEnterprise applications
Annotation SupportLimitedFull

When to Use BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext

🏗️

Use BeanFactory when

Memory is very limited.
Building a very small, lightweight application.
Only basic IoC features are needed.

🏭

Use ApplicationContext when

Building enterprise-level applications.
AOP, events, or i18n are required.
Annotation-based configuration is used.
(This is the recommended choice in almost all cases.)

💡 Key Insight
In modern Spring development, ApplicationContext is almost always used. BeanFactory is rarely used today but understanding it helps you grasp the foundation of how Spring's IoC Container works.
Module 5 · Spring Bean Configuration · 5d · i

Using Annotations for Bean Configuration

The modern way to configure Spring beans — using Java annotations instead of XML, making code cleaner, shorter, and easier to maintain.

What are Annotations?

  • Annotations are special markers placed before a class, method, or variable in Java to provide metadata (additional information) to the compiler or framework.
  • They start with the @ symbol.
Java — Examples
@Override         // Java built-in annotation
@Component        // Spring annotation
@Autowired        // Spring annotation

Why Use Annotations Instead of XML?

❌

XML Configuration

Requires a separate beans.xml file.
More verbose — lots of tags.
Hard to maintain for large projects.
Refactoring is error-prone.

✅

Annotation Configuration

Configuration lives in the Java class itself.
Less code — cleaner and simpler.
Easy to maintain and refactor.
Modern standard approach.

Important Spring Annotations

🔖 1) @Component
  • Marks a class as a Spring Bean.
  • Spring automatically detects and registers it in the IoC Container.
  • No need to define the bean in XML.
Java
@Component
public class Student {
    private String name = "Vishal";
    // getters and setters
}
Spring automatically creates: Student student = new Student();
✅ 2) @Autowired
  • Tells Spring to automatically inject the required dependency.
  • Spring finds the matching bean and injects it automatically.
  • No need to manually create or assign the dependency.
Java
@Component
public class Car {
    @Autowired
    private Engine engine;
    // Spring automatically injects the Engine bean here
}
ℹ️ 3) @Configuration
  • Marks a class as a Java-based Spring configuration class.
  • Replaces the beans.xml file entirely.
  • Used together with @Bean methods.
Java
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    // Bean definitions go here
}
ℹ️ 4) @Bean
  • Declares a method that returns a Spring Bean.
  • Used inside @Configuration classes.
  • Spring calls this method and registers the returned object as a bean.
Java
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public Student student() {
        return new Student();
        // Spring registers this as a Bean named "student"
    }
}

Component Scanning

  • For Spring to detect @Component annotations, it must scan the package.
  • This is enabled using @ComponentScan in your configuration class or via XML.
Java — Enabling Component Scan
@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.example")
public class AppConfig {
    // Spring will scan com.example package for @Component classes
}

Complete Example — Annotation-Based Configuration

Engine.java

Java
@Component
public class Engine {
    public void start() {
        System.out.println("Engine Started");
    }
}

Car.java

Java
@Component
public class Car {

    @Autowired
    private Engine engine;  // Spring injects Engine automatically

    public void drive() {
        engine.start();
        System.out.println("Car is driving");
    }
}

AppConfig.java

Java
@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.example")
public class AppConfig {
    // No bean definitions needed — @Component handles it
}

Main.java

Java
import org.springframework.context.ApplicationContext;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.AnnotationConfigApplicationContext;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // Load configuration from AppConfig class (not XML)
        ApplicationContext context =
            new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);

        // Get Car bean
        Car car = context.getBean(Car.class);
        car.drive();
    }
}
ℹ️ Output
Engine Started
Car is driving

XML vs Annotation Configuration

FeatureXML ConfigurationAnnotation Configuration
Bean Definition<bean> in beans.xml@Component on the class
Dependency Injection<property> tag@Autowired on field
Configuration Classbeans.xml@Configuration class
Code AmountMore (separate XML file)Less (inside Java class)
ReadabilityXML is verboseAnnotations are concise
Refactoring SupportManualIDE-supported
Modern Approach❌ Old-style✅ Recommended

Advantages

Less code — no XML files Easier to read and maintain Better IDE support and refactoring Faster development Standard in modern Spring apps
Module 5 · Spring Bean Configuration · 5d · ii

Component Scanning

The process where Spring automatically searches packages for annotated classes and registers them as beans — no manual XML required.

What is Component Scanning?

Component Scanning is the process where Spring automatically searches packages for annotated classes and creates Beans for them.

ℹ️ How Does Spring Know?
Imagine your project contains 200 Java classes. How does Spring know which classes should become Beans? Does Spring check every class manually? No.

Instead, Spring scans the packages. Whenever it finds an annotation like @Component, it says: "This class should become a Bean."

Real-Life Analogy — School

School Analogy
The principal says: "Find all teachers."

The staff walks through every classroom. Whenever they see someone wearing a Teacher ID Card, they register them.

Mapping

Real LifeSpring
SchoolPackage
Teacher ID Card@Component
Staff SearchingComponent Scanning
Registered TeacherSpring Bean

Syntax

Java — AppConfig.java
@Configuration  // Marks this class as a configuration class
@ComponentScan("com.demo")  // Tells Spring which package to scan
public class AppConfig {

}
💡 What This Does
Spring will scan the com.demo package and all its sub-packages. Any class annotated with @Component (or @Service, @Repository, @Controller) will be registered as a Spring Bean automatically.

Advantages

Automatically discovers Beans Eliminates large XML files Faster development Cleaner project structure Preferred in modern Spring applications
Module 5 · Spring Bean Configuration · 5d · iii

@Component Annotation

The fundamental Spring stereotype annotation that marks a Java class as a Spring-managed Bean — the building block of annotation-based configuration.

What is @Component?

  • @Component is a Spring stereotype annotation used to mark a Java class as a Spring Bean.
  • When Spring performs Component Scanning, it detects classes annotated with @Component and registers them as Beans in the IoC Container.

Without vs With @Component

❌

Without @Component

Java
public class Student {

}

This is just a normal Java class. Spring ignores it.

✅

With @Component

Java
@Component
public class Student {

}

Now Spring understands: "This class should be managed by me."

What Happens After @Component?

Student Class with @Component
↓
Component Scan runs (@ComponentScan)
↓
Spring IoC Container detects the annotation
↓
Student Bean Created & Registered

@Component and Its Specializations

Spring provides specialized versions of @Component for different layers:

AnnotationLayerPurpose
@ComponentAnyGeneric Spring Bean
@ServiceService LayerBusiness logic
@RepositoryData LayerDatabase operations
@ControllerWeb LayerHandles HTTP requests
💡 All are @Component internally
@Service, @Repository, and @Controller are all specializations of @Component. They behave the same way but add semantic meaning to the code.

Advantages

Eliminates XML Bean definitions Cleaner and shorter code Automatic Bean registration Easy maintenance Widely used in Spring Boot
Module 5 · Spring Bean Configuration · 5d · iv

@Service Annotation

A Spring stereotype annotation that marks a class as the Service Layer — the home of business logic in a layered Spring application.

What is @Service?

  • @Service is a Spring stereotype annotation used to mark a class as a Service Bean.
  • It tells Spring: "This class contains business logic."
Online Shopping Example
Suppose you're building an Online Shopping Application. You have an OrderService class that contains logic like:

Calculate total price · Apply discount · Validate payment · Generate invoice

These operations are business logic. So we annotate it with @Service.
Java
@Service
public class OrderService {
    // business logic here
}

Now Spring knows: This class belongs to the Service Layer and should be managed as a Bean.

What is Business Logic?

  • Business logic is the part of the application that handles the core functionality and rules of the business domain.
  • It defines how data is created, stored, and changed.
  • Business Logic is the set of rules that determine how an application works.
ℹ️ Example — Banking App Business Logic
Transfer money · Check balance · Calculate interest · Validate account

Real-Life Analogy — Restaurant

Food Order Analogy
Customer → Waiter → Chef → Kitchen

The Chef does the actual cooking.
Similarly, the @Service performs the application's actual work.

Mapping

Real LifeSpring
CustomerUser
Waiter@Controller
Chef@Service
Kitchen@Repository

Syntax

Java
@Service
public class StudentService {
    // business logic methods go here
}

Advantages

Clearly identifies the business layer Improves project readability Better separation of concerns Easy to maintain Widely used in enterprise applications
Module 5 · Spring Bean Configuration · 5d · v

@Repository Annotation

A Spring stereotype annotation that marks the data access layer — the class responsible for all database communication in a layered application.

What is @Repository?

  • @Repository is a Spring stereotype annotation used to mark a class that communicates with the database.
  • It tells Spring: "This class is responsible for database operations."

Example — Student Management System

Suppose you're building a Student Management System. You need to:

Save student details Update student details Delete student records Find a student by ID

Which class should do these database operations? A class annotated with @Repository:

Java
@Repository
public class StudentRepository {

    public void save(Student student) {
        // Insert student into database
    }

    public Student findById(int id) {
        // Read one student record by ID
        return null;
    }

    public void delete(int id) {
        // Remove student record from database
    }
}

Common Database Operations

MethodOperation
save()Insert data
findById()Read one record
findAll()Read all records
update()Modify data
delete()Remove data
💡 Where @Repository Sits in the Layers
LayerAnnotationResponsibility
Web Layer@ControllerHandle HTTP requests
Service Layer@ServiceBusiness logic
Data Layer@RepositoryDatabase operations

Advantages

  • Separates database code from business logic.
  • Improves maintainability.
  • Makes testing easier.
  • Organizes code according to layered architecture.
  • Spring provides automatic exception translation for repository classes.
Module 5 · Spring Bean Configuration · 5d · vi

@Controller Annotation

A Spring stereotype annotation that marks the web layer — the class responsible for receiving user requests, delegating to the service, and returning responses.

What is @Controller?

  • @Controller is a Spring stereotype annotation used to mark a class that handles user requests.
  • It is the entry point of every incoming HTTP request in a Spring web application.

Real-Life Example — Online Shopping

Online Shopping Website
Imagine you're using an online shopping website. You click Login or Buy Now.

Who receives that request? The Controller.
❌

Controller Does NOT

Calculate discounts
Save data to the database

✅

Controller DOES

Receives the HTTP request
Calls the Service layer
Returns the response to the user

Syntax

Java
@Controller
public class StudentController {
    // handles incoming web requests
}

Full Layer Flow Diagram

User sends HTTP Request
↓
@Controller — Receives request, calls Service
↓
@Service — Executes business logic
↓
@Repository — Communicates with Database
↓
Database
↑
Response returned back to User

All Stereotype Annotations — Summary

AnnotationLayerResponsibility
@Controller Web Layer Receives HTTP requests, returns responses
@Service Service Layer Contains business logic
@Repository Data Layer Communicates with the database
@Component Any Layer Generic Spring Bean (base of all above)
💡 Key Insight
All four annotations — @Controller, @Service, @Repository — are specialized forms of @Component. They all register the class as a Spring Bean, but add semantic meaning to the architecture.

Advantages

Separates request handling from business logic Improves code organization Easier testing Supports MVC architecture Makes applications easier to maintain
Module 5 · Spring Bean Configuration · 5d · vii

Java-based Configuration using @Configuration

Using a Java class instead of an XML file to configure the Spring IoC Container — more type-safe, IDE-friendly, and the modern standard.

What is Java-based Configuration?

Java-based Configuration means using Java classes instead of XML files to configure the Spring IoC Container.

📄

Old Way — XML Approach

beans.xml
<bean id="student"
      class="com.demo.Student"/>
☕

New Way — Java Approach

Java — AppConfig.java
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

}

This Java class replaces most of the work previously done by beans.xml.

What is @Configuration?

  • @Configuration is a Spring annotation that marks a Java class as a Configuration Class.
  • It tells Spring: "This class contains Bean definitions and configuration information."

Real-Life Analogy

📝

Old Method — Paper Instructions

Go Left → Go Right → Turn Right

This is like XML — static, hard to update, no instant feedback.

🗺️

Modern Method — Google Maps

Dynamic, interactive, recalculates in real time.

This is like Java Configuration — more interactive and easier to maintain.

How @Configuration Works

Java — Full Example
@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.demo")
public class AppConfig {

    // Optionally define beans manually using @Bean
    @Bean
    public Student student() {
        return new Student();
    }
}
ℹ️ Loading Java Configuration
Instead of ClassPathXmlApplicationContext, use AnnotationConfigApplicationContext:
Java — Main.java
ApplicationContext context =
    new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);

Student student = context.getBean(Student.class);

XML Configuration vs Java-based Configuration

FeatureXML ConfigurationJava @Configuration
LanguageXMLJava
Type Safety❌ No (runtime errors)✅ Yes (compile-time)
IDE SupportLimitedFull (autocomplete, refactor)
ReadabilityVerbose XML tagsClean Java code
RefactoringManualIDE-assisted
Modern UsageLegacy projectsSpring & Spring Boot

Advantages

No XML required Type-safe — checked by the Java compiler Better IDE support Easier refactoring Preferred in Spring Boot
Module 5 · Spring Bean Configuration · 5d · viii

Mixing XML and Java-based Configurations

Using both XML and Java-based configurations in the same Spring application — the bridge between legacy and modern Spring projects.

What is Mixing XML and Java-based Configurations?

  • A feature in Spring that allows you to use both XML and Java-based configurations in the same application.
  • You can define some beans in XML and others in Java configuration classes.
  • This is useful when you want to gradually migrate from XML to Java configuration or when different teams prefer different approaches.

Example

XML Configuration (beans.xml)

beans.xml
<bean id="student" class="com.example.Student"/>

Java Configuration (AppConfig.java)

Java
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    @Bean
    public Teacher teacher() {
        return new Teacher();
    }
}
ℹ️ Result
The Student bean is defined in XML, and the Teacher bean is defined in Java. Both are available in the same Spring IoC Container.

Why Do We Need Mixed Configuration?

Banking Application — Real World Scenario
Imagine a banking application developed in 2015. It has a beans.xml with 500 Bean Definitions. Now the company upgrades to Spring Boot.

Should developers rewrite everything? That would take a lot of time and introduce risk.

Instead, they can gradually migrate:
Old XML Beans + New Java Configuration → Same Application

This gradual transition is called Hybrid Configuration. Key reasons to use it:

Gradual Migration — step by step from XML to Java Team Preferences — different teams may prefer different styles Legacy Code — some parts still use XML Flexibility — choose best approach per module

How Spring Handles Both

Diagram
            Spring Application
                    │
    ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
    │                               │
    ▼                               ▼
beans.xml                   AppConfig.java
    │                               │
    └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                    ▼
          Spring IoC Container
                    │
                    ▼
             All Beans Available

When Do We Use Hybrid Configuration?

CaseScenario
Case 1Large enterprise project — thousands of XML Beans already exist.
Case 2Company gradually migrates to Spring Boot.
Case 3Third-party framework provides XML configuration.
Case 4Legacy project maintenance.

Advantages

Easy migration from XML to Java No need to rewrite old projects immediately Supports legacy applications Flexible configuration Smooth transition to modern Spring
Module 5 · Dependency Injection · 5e · i

Introduction to Dependency Injection (DI)

A design pattern where objects receive their dependencies from external sources — the foundation of loose coupling in Spring applications.

What is Dependency Injection (DI)?

  • Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern where objects receive their dependencies from external sources rather than creating them itself.
  • It promotes loose coupling and makes code more modular and testable.
  • In Spring, DI is achieved through the Inversion of Control (IoC) container.
Car & Engine
Suppose we have two classes: Car and Engine. A Car cannot run without an Engine. So, Car depends on Engine.

Instead of writing Engine engine = new Engine(); inside Car — Spring automatically provides the Engine object to the Car.

This is called Dependency Injection.

What is a Dependency?

  • A dependency is an object that a class needs to function.
  • For example, a Car needs an Engine to run.
  • The Engine is a dependency of the Car.

What is Injection?

  • Injection means providing the dependency to the class.
  • Instead of the class creating the dependency, it is provided from outside.
  • This is done by the Spring IoC Container.

Why Do We Need Dependency Injection?

Imagine a project with: 200 Services · 100 Repositories · 50 Utility Classes.

❌

Without DI

Java
new StudentRepository();
new EmployeeRepository();
new PaymentRepository();

Every class creates its own dependencies.

✅

With DI

Spring IoC Container → Creates Repository → Injects into Service.

The developer focuses on business logic, not object creation.

Problems Without DI

Tight Coupling Difficult Testing Difficult Maintenance Code Duplication

Code Example — Without DI vs With DI

Without DI — Tight Coupling

Java
class Engine {
    public void start() {
        System.out.println("Engine Started");
    }
}

class Car {
    // Car creates its own dependency (Tight Coupling)
    Engine engine = new Engine();

    public void drive() {
        engine.start();
        System.out.println("Car Running");
    }
}
⚠️ Problem
Car is tightly coupled to Engine. If you want to change the Engine type (e.g., ElectricEngine), you must modify the Car class itself.

With DI — Loose Coupling

Java
class Engine {
    public void start() {
        System.out.println("Engine Started");
    }
}

class Car {
    private Engine engine;

    // Dependency is provided from outside (DI)
    public Car(Engine engine) {
        this.engine = engine;
    }

    public void drive() {
        engine.start();
        System.out.println("Car Running");
    }
}
💡 With DI
Car no longer creates Engine. The Engine is injected from outside. You can easily swap it with ElectricEngine or DieselEngine without touching the Car class.

Advantages

Reduces Tight Coupling Promotes Loose Coupling Easier Testing — dependencies can be mocked Better Maintainability Reusable code Easier to modify and extend
Module 5 · Dependency Injection · 5e · ii

Using @Resource and @Inject Annotations

Java standard alternatives to Spring's @Autowired — for code that should remain portable across different DI frameworks.

What is @Inject?

  • @Inject is a standard Java Dependency Injection annotation defined by JSR-330.
  • Spring supports it just like @Autowired.
  • It injects beans by type — same behaviour as @Autowired.

What is @Resource?

  • @Resource is a Jakarta annotation used for dependency injection.
  • Unlike @Autowired, it primarily injects beans by their name.
  • It is part of the Java EE / Jakarta EE standard.

Why Do We Need @Inject and @Resource?

ℹ️ The Reason
Spring has its own annotation: @Autowired.

But what if you want your code to follow Java standards instead of using Spring-specific annotations? Then you can use @Inject or @Resource.

Spring understands these annotations and performs dependency injection exactly the same way.

Real-Life Analogy — School

Two Students — Rahul & Rohit
There are two students named Rahul and Rohit.
🔍

By Type — @Autowired / @Inject

Teacher says: "Call a student."

If only one student matches → easy.
If many match → confusion occurs.

🏷️

By Name — @Resource

Teacher says: "Call Rahul."

No confusion — the exact bean is targeted by name.

@Autowired vs @Inject vs @Resource

Feature@Autowired@Inject@Resource
SourceSpringJSR-330 (Java Standard)Jakarta EE (Java Standard)
Injects ByTypeTypeName (by default)
Spring Support✅ Native✅ Supported✅ Supported
PortabilitySpring onlyAny JSR-330 frameworkAny Jakarta EE container
Ambiguity HandlingUse @QualifierUse @NamedUse name attribute

Syntax

Using @Inject

Java
import jakarta.inject.Inject;

@Component
public class Car {

    @Inject
    private Engine engine;  // Injected by type
}

Using @Resource

Java
import jakarta.annotation.Resource;

@Component
public class Car {

    @Resource(name = "petrolEngine")
    private Engine engine;  // Injected by name: "petrolEngine"
}

Advantages

💉

@Inject Advantages

Java standard annotation.
Portable across DI frameworks.
Works well with Spring.

🏷️

@Resource Advantages

Good when you know the Bean name.
Helps avoid ambiguity.
Java standard (Jakarta EE).

Module 5 · Dependency Injection · 5e · iii

Constructor Injection

Spring provides the required dependency through the constructor of a class — the recommended approach for mandatory dependencies.

What is Constructor Injection?

Constructor Injection is a type of Dependency Injection where Spring provides the required dependency through the constructor of a class.

Car & Engine
A Car cannot run without an Engine. Instead of the Car creating its own Engine, Spring provides the Engine while creating the Car.
❌

Without Spring

Java
Engine engine = new Engine();
Car car = new Car(engine);

Developer manually creates and passes dependencies.

✅

With Spring

Spring IoC Container
↓ Creates Engine Bean
↓ Passes Engine to Car Constructor
↓ Creates Car Bean

Why Do We Need Constructor Injection?

Without Constructor Injection

Java — Tight Coupling
class Car {
    Engine engine = new Engine();  // Tight Coupling
}
Tight Coupling Hard to test Hard to replace Engine implementation

With Constructor Injection

Java — Loose Coupling
class Car {
    private Engine engine;

    public Car(Engine engine) {
        this.engine = engine;
    }
}

Now, Car doesn't create the Engine. Spring provides it.

Real-Life Analogy — Buying a Car

Car Delivery Analogy
When you receive a new car, the engine is already installed. You don't buy the engine separately and install it yourself.
Real LifeSpring
Car CompanySpring IoC Container
EngineDependency
CarMain Bean
Engine installed before deliveryConstructor Injection

Complete Code Example

Engine.java

Java
public class Engine {
    public void start() {
        System.out.println("Engine Started");
    }
}

Car.java

Java
public class Car {
    private Engine engine;

    // Constructor for injecting Engine
    public Car(Engine engine) {
        this.engine = engine;
    }

    public void drive() {
        engine.start();
        System.out.println("Car is running");
    }
}

Main.java

Java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Spring would handle this automatically
        Engine engine = new Engine();
        Car car = new Car(engine);
        car.drive();
    }
}

XML Constructor Injection

Older Spring projects use XML:

beans.xml
<bean id="engine"
      class="com.demo.Engine"/>

<bean id="car"
      class="com.demo.Car">
    <constructor-arg ref="engine"/>
</bean>

Understanding <constructor-arg>

AttributePurpose
constructor-argPasses a constructor argument to the bean
ref="engine"References the Engine Bean by its id
ℹ️ What Spring Does Internally
new Car(engine);

Advantages

Promotes Loose Coupling Mandatory dependencies always initialized Easier unit testing Supports immutable objects (dependencies can be final) Recommended by Spring for required dependencies
Module 5 · Dependency Injection · 5e · iv

Setter Injection

Spring injects the required dependency through a setter method — ideal for optional dependencies that can be changed or configured after object creation.

What is Setter Injection?

Setter Injection is a type of Dependency Injection where Spring injects the required dependency through a setter method.

🏗️

Constructor Injection

Java
Car car = new Car(engine);
// Dependency during creation
🔧

Setter Injection

Java
Car car = new Car();
car.setEngine(engine);
// Dependency after creation

Real-Life Analogy — Desktop Computer

Computer & Accessories
Imagine buying a desktop computer. When you buy it, you just get the computer. Later you install: Printer · Webcam · Speakers.

These accessories are added after purchasing the computer.

Unlike Constructor Injection, the dependency is not provided during object creation.

Mapping

Real LifeSpring
ComputerCar Bean (main object)
Printer / WebcamDependency
Install LaterSetter Injection

Code Example

Engine.java

Java
public class Engine {
    public void start() {
        System.out.println("Engine Started");
    }
}

Car.java

Java
public class Car {
    private Engine engine;

    // Setter method — Spring calls this to inject the dependency
    public void setEngine(Engine engine) {
        this.engine = engine;
    }

    public void drive() {
        engine.start();
        System.out.println("Car is running");
    }
}

XML Configuration (beans.xml)

beans.xml
<bean id="engine" class="com.demo.Engine"/>

<bean id="car" class="com.demo.Car">
    <property name="engine" ref="engine"/>
</bean>
ℹ️ What Spring Does Internally
Car car = new Car();
car.setEngine(engine);

Constructor Injection vs Setter Injection

FeatureConstructor InjectionSetter Injection
When injectedDuring object creationAfter object creation
Dependency typeMandatory dependenciesOptional dependencies
Immutability✅ Supports (use final)❌ Not supported
FlexibilityLess flexibleMore flexible
Spring recommendation✅ PreferredFor optional deps only
XML tag<constructor-arg><property>

Advantages

Suitable for optional dependencies Dependency can be changed later Easier to configure in some scenarios More flexible than Constructor Injection
Module 5 · Dependency Injection · 5e · v

Autowiring Dependencies (@Autowired)

Spring automatically finds and injects the required bean — no manual XML configuration needed. The most widely used DI mechanism in modern Spring.

What is @Autowired?

  • @Autowired is a Spring annotation used to automatically inject a required Bean into another Bean.
  • Spring finds the matching Bean by type and injects it — no manual wiring required.
📄

Before @Autowired

Explicit configuration required every time:

XML
<!-- Constructor -->
<constructor-arg ref="engine"/>
<!-- OR Setter -->
<property name="engine" ref="engine"/>
⚡

With @Autowired

Spring does it automatically:

Java
@Autowired
private Engine engine;

Spring says: "I will find the Engine Bean and inject it automatically."

Real-Life Analogy — Hotel

Hotel Room Analogy
Imagine a hotel. You book a room. You don't bring: Bed · Chair · AC · TV.

The hotel automatically provides them.
Real LifeSpring
HotelSpring IoC Container
RoomCar Bean
FurnitureDependencies
Automatic Room Setup@Autowired

Three Ways to Use @Autowired

🔖 1. Field Injection
Spring injects the dependency directly into the field.
Java
@Component
public class Car {
    @Autowired
    private Engine engine;
}
ℹ️ 2. Setter Injection
Spring calls the setter method automatically.
Java
@Component
public class Car {
    private Engine engine;

    @Autowired
    public void setEngine(Engine engine) {
        this.engine = engine;
    }
}
⭐ 3. Constructor Injection (Recommended)
Spring injects through the constructor — supports immutable fields with final.
Java
@Component
public class Car {
    private final Engine engine;

    @Autowired
    public Car(Engine engine) {
        this.engine = engine;
    }
}

Modern Spring (4.3+) — @Autowired Optional

In modern Spring (4.3+), if a class has only one constructor, @Autowired can even be omitted. Spring still performs constructor injection automatically.

Java — @Autowired omitted (Spring 4.3+)
@Component
public class Car {
    private final Engine engine;

    // No @Autowired needed — Spring detects single constructor automatically
    public Car(Engine engine) {
        this.engine = engine;
    }
}

Comparison — Three @Autowired Injection Types

TypeWhere @AutowiredRecommended?Supports final?
Field InjectionOn the field❌ Not preferred❌ No
Setter InjectionOn the setter methodFor optional deps❌ No
Constructor InjectionOn the constructor⭐ Recommended✅ Yes

Advantages

Automatic dependency injection Less XML configuration Cleaner code Easier maintenance Widely used in Spring Boot
Module 5 · Dependency Injection · 5e · vi

Qualifiers for Resolving Autowiring Conflicts (@Qualifier)

When multiple beans of the same type exist, @Qualifier tells Spring exactly which one to inject — preventing NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.

What is @Qualifier?

  • @Qualifier is a Spring annotation used along with @Autowired to specify which Bean should be injected when multiple Beans of the same type exist.

The Problem — Ambiguous Beans

Suppose you have two Engine Beans: PetrolEngine and DieselEngine.

Bean Hierarchy
Engine
│
├── PetrolEngine
│
└── DieselEngine

Now your Car needs an Engine. Spring asks: "Which one should I use?" — It cannot decide.

⚠️ Result Without @Qualifier
Spring finds both PetrolEngine Bean and DieselEngine Bean. Both match the type Engine.

Spring throws an exception: NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException

Solution — Use @Qualifier

Java
@Component
public class Car {

    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("petrolEngine")
    private Engine engine;
    // Spring now knows: inject the PetrolEngine Bean
}
💡 What This Tells Spring
