Advantages

Minimal configuration needed Automatic bean creation Faster development Easy environment-specific settings No recompilation for config changes Enterprise-ready with multiple data sources Less boilerplate code
Module 6 · Spring Data JPA · 6j

Spring Data JPA and Hibernate

Hibernate is the engine under the hood — implementing every JPA rule, generating SQL, tracking changes, caching results, and loading related data on demand.

What is Hibernate?

  • Hibernate is an ORM (Object Relational Mapping) Framework that implements the JPA Specification.
  • It acts as a bridge between the Java Application and the Relational Database — converting Java Objects ↔ Database Records automatically.

Who Does What?

TechnologyResponsibility
Spring BootAuto-configuration of everything
Spring Data JPASimplifies database access (Repository abstraction)
JPADefines the persistence specification (rules)
HibernateImplements JPA rules · Generates SQL · Executes queries
DatabaseStores data permanently

Why Do We Need Hibernate?

❌

Without Hibernate

Developer manually writes:
SQL · JDBC code · Object mapping · Connection handling

Hundreds of repetitive lines.

✅

With Hibernate

Automatically:
Maps objects to tables · Generates SQL · Executes queries · Manages caching · Handles transactions · Supports lazy loading

Hibernate-Specific Features

FeaturePurpose
Automatic SQL GenerationGenerates SQL automatically from entity operations
Dirty CheckingDetects changed objects and auto-updates DB
CachingImproves performance by storing data in memory
Lazy LoadingLoads related data only when accessed
Eager LoadingLoads all related data immediately
Batch ProcessingExecutes multiple operations in one batch
HQLHibernate Query Language — object-oriented querying
Dialect SupportGenerates correct SQL for different databases

Dirty Checking

Hibernate automatically detects changes made to managed entities and generates UPDATE queries at transaction commit — no manual update call needed.

Employee salary: 50000
↓
Developer changes to: 60000
↓
Hibernate detects the change (Dirty Checking)
↓
UPDATE query auto-generated at transaction commit

Lazy Loading vs Eager Loading

😴

Lazy Loading

Related data is fetched only when accessed.

Employee loaded → Department fetched only if you access employee.getDepartment()

Faster initial load · Lower memory usage.

⚡

Eager Loading

Related data is fetched immediately with the parent.

Employee + Department loaded together in one query.

All data ready upfront.

Caching

Caching stores frequently used data in memory. Instead of querying the database every time, Hibernate retrieves from cache when possible.

❌

Without Cache

Every request → Database → Database → Database

High database load.

✅

With Cache

Request → Cache (if available) → Database (only if needed)

Database load reduced significantly.

HQL — Hibernate Query Language

HQL is similar to JPQL — it uses Entity names and fields instead of table/column names, making it database-independent.

🗄️

SQL

SQL
SELECT * FROM employee
WHERE salary > 50000

Uses table name

☕

HQL

HQL
FROM Employee e
WHERE e.salary > 50000

Uses Entity name

Batch Processing

Hibernate groups multiple operations into batches for far better performance with large datasets.

College Student Admission
Without Batch: Insert 500 students one by one → 500 database trips.

With Batch: Insert all 500 in one batch → 1 database trip.

Much faster. Useful for: Bulk inserts · Bulk updates · Bulk deletes.
Reduced network overhead Improved throughput Better resource utilization

Hibernate-Specific Annotations

AnnotationPurpose
@CreationTimestampAutomatically stores creation timestamp
@UpdateTimestampAutomatically stores last update timestamp
@DynamicInsertGenerates INSERT SQL with only non-null columns
@DynamicUpdateUpdates only the modified columns (not all)

Hibernate Dialect

A Dialect tells Hibernate which SQL syntax to generate for a specific database — since MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL all have slightly different SQL syntax.

ℹ️ Example
MySQL: LIMIT 10
Oracle: FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY

Hibernate handles these differences automatically through the configured Dialect.

Common Hibernate Properties

PropertyPurpose
hibernate.dialectSpecifies the database dialect
hibernate.show_sqlDisplay generated SQL in console
hibernate.format_sqlFormat SQL output for readability
hibernate.hbm2ddl.autoDatabase schema management (update/create/validate)

Advantages

Automatic SQL generation ORM support — no manual mapping Database independence via Dialect Automatic dirty checking Built-in caching for performance Lazy loading reduces memory Batch processing for bulk ops Enterprise-ready
Module 7 · Spring REST · 7a

Introduction to Spring REST and Spring Boot 3

REST is the architectural style powering the modern web — and Spring Boot 3 makes building RESTful APIs fast, clean, and production-ready with minimal configuration.

What is REST?

  • REST stands for Representational State Transfer — an architectural style for building communication between clients and servers over HTTP.
  • REST is not a language, not a framework, not a protocol — it is a set of architectural principles.
  • It enables different systems (mobile apps, websites, desktop apps) to communicate easily.

Real-World Example — Swiggy

Swiggy App — REST in Action
When you open the app: GET /restaurants → Server returns restaurant list
When you place an order: POST /orders → Server creates order
When you cancel: DELETE /orders/25 → Order deleted

Everything happens using HTTP. This is REST.

REST Architecture

🌐 Client (Browser · Mobile App · React · Flutter)
↓ HTTP Request
⚙️ REST API Server (Spring Boot · Controllers · Services · Repository)
↓
🗄️ Database (MySQL · PostgreSQL)

Internal Request Flow

1. Client sends HTTP Request: GET /employees
↓
2. Spring Boot receives request via DispatcherServlet
↓
3. Controller method invoked · Service called · Repository fetches data
↓
4. Response returned as JSON · Client receives JSON

Why Do We Need REST?

❌

Before REST (SOAP / RPC)

Complex · Heavy XML messages · Difficult to maintain · Slow · Tight coupling

✅

REST Introduced

Simplicity · Lightweight communication · HTTP support · JSON · Scalability

REST Constraints (6 Principles)

🔖 1. Client-Server
Client and Server are separate and independent. React app ↔ Spring Boot ↔ Database.
Advantage: Independent development — frontend and backend can evolve separately.
🔖 2. Stateless
Every request is independent. The server stores no client session.
Each request must contain all required info (e.g., JWT token) — the server doesn't remember previous requests.
🔖 3. Cacheable
Responses may be cached. Example: GET /countries — no need to request every time. Improves performance.
🔖 4. Uniform Interface
Every REST API follows similar URL and method rules.
GET /users · POST /users · PUT /users/10 · DELETE /users/10 — easy to understand.
🔖 5. Layered System
The client never knows if the request goes through a load balancer, gateway, security layer, or directly to the app. All layers are transparent.
🔖 6. Code on Demand (Optional)
Server may send executable code (e.g. JavaScript). Rarely used today.

HTTP Methods

MethodPurposeURI Example
GETRead dataGET /students
POSTCreate dataPOST /students
PUTUpdate entire resourcePUT /students/10
PATCHPartial updatePATCH /students/10
DELETEDelete resourceDELETE /students/10

HTTP Status Codes

CodeMeaning
200OK — Request successful
201Created — Resource created successfully
204No Content — Success, but no body returned
400Bad Request — Invalid input
401Unauthorized — Authentication required
403Forbidden — No permission
404Not Found — Resource doesn't exist
500Internal Server Error — Server-side failure

Introduction to Spring REST

  • Spring REST is Spring's support for building RESTful web services using annotations like @RestController.
  • Spring REST handles: receiving HTTP requests · routing · Java ↔ JSON conversion (serialization/deserialization) · sending HTTP responses.

Common Spring REST Annotations

AnnotationPurposeExample
@RestControllerMarks class as REST controller@RestController
@RequestMappingMaps base URL / groups endpoints@RequestMapping("/api")
@GetMappingMaps GET request@GetMapping("/users")
@PostMappingMaps POST request@PostMapping("/users")
@PutMappingMaps PUT request@PutMapping("/users/{id}")
@DeleteMappingMaps DELETE request@DeleteMapping("/users/{id}")

Complete Example — @RestController

Java — EmployeeController.java
@RestController              // Marks this class as a REST Controller
@RequestMapping("/api")      // Base URL for all endpoints
public class EmployeeController {

    @GetMapping("/employees")   // Handles GET /api/employees
    public String getEmployees() {
        return "Employee List";   // Returned directly as HTTP response
    }
}

What's New in Spring Boot 3?

FeatureDescription
Java 17+ RequiredMinimum supported Java version is 17
Jakarta EE 9Package names changed: javax.* → jakarta.*
Spring Framework 6Built on the latest Spring Framework
Native SupportBetter GraalVM native image support
Better ObservabilityEnhanced metrics, tracing, and monitoring
Security UpdatesImproved Spring Security 6 integration
⚠️ Key Migration Note
If upgrading from Spring Boot 2 to 3: replace all javax.* imports with jakarta.* — this is the most common breaking change.

Standard REST Project Architecture

Project Structure
src/main/java
├── controller    ← Receives HTTP requests
├── service       ← Contains business logic
├── repository    ← Communicates with database
├── entity        ← Represents database tables
└── dto           ← Transfers data between client and server

src/main/resources
└── application.properties

Benefits of Spring Boot for REST

BenefitExplanation
Auto-ConfigurationConfigures components automatically from classpath
Embedded ServerBuilt-in Tomcat — no external deployment needed
Starter DependenciesOne starter pulls in all required libraries
JSON SupportJackson integrated by default for serialization
Production ReadyActuator, Metrics, Health Checks built-in
Easy TestingStrong support via Spring Test and MockMvc

Advantages

Lightweight and easy to understand Platform independent Stateless — highly scalable JSON support via Jackson Standard HTTP — universal client support Production-ready with Spring Boot 3 Ideal for microservices
Module 7 · Spring REST · 7b

Building a Simple REST Controller

A REST Controller receives HTTP requests and returns data (JSON) directly — not a webpage. It's the entry point of every REST API.

Spring MVC vs Spring REST — Key Difference

🌐

Spring MVC Controller

Receives request → Returns a View (JSP / Thymeleaf)

Used for web pages.

📡

Spring REST Controller

Receives request → Returns Data (JSON / XML)

Used for APIs.

ℹ️ This is the biggest conceptual difference between MVC and REST.

Restaurant Analogy

RestaurantREST Application
CustomerClient (Browser / Mobile App)
WaiterREST Controller
ChefService Layer
KitchenDatabase

@RestController

@RestController combines @Controller + @ResponseBody. Every method returns data directly — not a View.

Java — Syntax
@RestController
public class EmployeeController {

}
Feature@Controller@RestController
ReturnsView (JSP / Thymeleaf)JSON / XML data
Used forWeb pagesAPIs
View Resolver✅ Used❌ Not needed
ClientsBrowserReact · Flutter · Android · iOS

Defining Request Mappings

A Request Mapping tells Spring: "When this URL is requested, execute this Java method."

Java — Class-Level @RequestMapping
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/employees")
public class EmployeeController {
    // All endpoints now start with /employees
}
AnnotationPurpose
@RequestMappingGeneric mapping (any HTTP method)
@GetMappingGET — retrieve data
@PostMappingPOST — create data
@PutMappingPUT — update entire resource
@DeleteMappingDELETE — remove resource
@PatchMappingPATCH — partial update

Handling HTTP Methods — Examples

1) GET — Retrieve Data

Java
@GetMapping("/employees")
public String getEmployees() {
    return "Employee List";  // Executes on GET /employees
}

2) POST — Create Data

Java
@PostMapping("/employees")
public String createEmployee() {
    return "Employee Created";  // Executes on POST /employees
}

3) PUT — Update Entire Resource

Java
@PutMapping("/employees")
public String updateEmployee() {
    return "Employee Updated";  // Executes on PUT /employees
}

4) DELETE — Remove Data

Java
@DeleteMapping("/employees")
public String deleteEmployee() {
    return "Employee Deleted";  // Executes on DELETE /employees
}

5) PATCH — Partial Update

Java
@PatchMapping("/employees")
public String partialUpdateEmployee() {
    return "Employee Partially Updated";
}

Returning JSON Responses

REST APIs usually return JSON — lightweight, human-readable, language-independent, easy to parse.

Controller returns Java Object: new Employee(101, "Vishal")
↓
Spring Boot invokes Jackson automatically
↓
Jackson serializes Java object → JSON
↓
JSON written to HTTP response body
↓
Client (React / Flutter / Android) receives JSON

Complete JSON Example

Java — Employee POJO
class Employee {
    private int id;
    private String name;
    // Constructors, Getters and Setters
}
Java — Controller returning Object
@RestController
public class EmployeeController {

    @GetMapping("/employee")
    public Employee getEmployee() {
        return new Employee(101, "Vishal");
    }
}
JSON — HTTP Response
{
  "id": 101,
  "name": "Vishal"
}
💡 You never write JSON manually
Spring Boot + Jackson handles the conversion automatically. You just return Java objects.

Advantages

Clear separation between client and server Annotation-based — minimal boilerplate Automatic URL routing Auto JSON conversion via Jackson Works with React · Angular · Flutter · Android · iOS Easy testing with Postman / MockMvc Foundation for Microservices
Module 7 · Spring REST · 7c

Request and Response Handling

How a REST Controller receives data from clients — through URL path variables, query parameters, and request bodies — and how to send back meaningful responses and errors.

What is Request and Response Handling?

  • The process of receiving data from the client, processing it, executing business logic, and returning an appropriate response.
  • It is one of the core responsibilities of a REST Controller.
⚠️ Why It Matters
Without Request Handling → No API can receive user input.
Without Response Handling → Client never receives useful information.

Handling Path Variables — @PathVariable

Path Variables are values embedded inside the URL path — used to identify specific resources.

Hotel Room Analogy
Rooms: 101 · 102 · 103

"Take me to Room 103" → Room Number 103 is the Path Variable.

Similarly: GET /employees/123 → 123 is the employee ID path variable.
Java — @PathVariable Example
@GetMapping("/employees/{id}")
public Employee getEmployeeById(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return employeeService.getEmployeeById(id);
    // GET /employees/123 → id = 123
}

Handling Query Parameters — @RequestParam

Query Parameters are additional information sent after ? in the URL — used for searching, filtering, sorting, and pagination.

/search?name=Vishal /products?page=2 /products?sort=price /products?category=Laptop
Java — @RequestParam Example
@GetMapping("/search")
public String search(@RequestParam String name) {
    return "Searching : " + name;
}
// Request:  GET /search?name=Vishal
// Response: Searching : Vishal

@PathVariable vs @RequestParam

Feature@PathVariable@RequestParam
PositionInside URL pathAfter ? in URL
Required?MandatoryOptional
Used forIdentifying a resourceFiltering / searching / pagination
Example/employees/10/employees?page=2

Request Body Processing — @RequestBody

The Request Body contains data sent by the client — usually as JSON. Spring automatically converts it into a Java object.

Java — @RequestBody Example
@PostMapping("/employees")
public String saveEmployee(@RequestBody Employee employee) {
    return employee.getName();
}

// JSON Request Body:
// { "id": 101, "name": "Vishal" }
// Output: Vishal

Serialization vs Deserialization

📤

Serialization

Java Object → JSON

Happens on the Response (sending data out).

Employee → {"id":101, "name":"Vishal"}

📥

Deserialization

JSON → Java Object

Happens on the Request (receiving data in).

{"name":"Vishal"} → Employee

Form Data Processing

Sometimes data arrives from HTML forms instead of JSON. Use @RequestParam or @ModelAttribute.

Java — Form Data with @RequestParam
@PostMapping("/register")
public String register(
        @RequestParam String name,
        @RequestParam int age) {
    return "Registered";
}
FeatureJSON Body (@RequestBody)Form Data (@RequestParam)
Sent byAPI clients (Postman, React)HTML forms
FormatStructured JSONKey-value pairs
File uploadNot typical✅ Multipart form data

Exception Handling in REST Controllers

Without proper exception handling, clients receive confusing 500 Internal Server Error stack traces. Instead, return meaningful JSON error messages.

❌

Without Exception Handling

Response
500 Internal Server Error
java.lang.NullPointerException: ...

User gets confusing errors.

✅

With Exception Handling

JSON Response
{
  "message": "Employee Not Found"
}

Clean, meaningful error.

AnnotationPurpose
@ExceptionHandlerHandle specific exceptions inside one Controller
@ControllerAdviceGlobal exception handling across all Controllers
@RestControllerAdviceGlobal exception handling for REST APIs — returns JSON automatically

Advantages

Clean request processing Automatic data binding Automatic JSON conversion Better API design Flexible HTTP response customization Centralized error handling Meaningful error messages for clients
Module 7 · Spring REST · 7d

RESTful Resource Representation with DTOs

Never expose your database entities directly to the client. DTOs give you control over what data travels across the wire — hiding sensitive fields, reducing payload, and decoupling your API from your database.

Why Not Return the Entity Directly?

Employee Table — Sensitive Data Problem
IDNameSalaryPasswordAadhaarEmail
101Vishal50000abc123XXXXXv@gmail.com

If we return the full Entity: password, aadhaar, salary all exposed — serious security risk.

Instead, we return only: id · name · email — using a DTO.

What is a DTO?

  • A DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a simple Java object used to transfer only the required data between layers or between server and client.
  • A DTO does not contain business logic — it mainly stores data.
  • Think of a DTO as a filtered copy of an Entity — exposes only what the client needs.

Entity vs DTO

FeatureEntityDTO
RepresentsDatabase TableAPI Data (what client sees)
Connected toJPA / HibernateIndependent of database
FieldsAll table columnsOnly required fields
Used insideApplication internalsSent to/from client
TypePersistent ObjectTransfer Object

Code Example — Entity vs DTO

🗄️

Entity (All fields)

Java
@Entity
public class Employee {
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String password; // ⚠️
    private String aadhaar;  // ⚠️
    private String email;
}
📦

DTO (Safe fields only)

Java
public class EmployeeDTO {
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String email;
    // password & aadhaar removed ✅
}

Mapping Entities to DTOs

Mapping = converting an Entity object into a DTO object (and vice versa).

1) Manual Mapping

Java
EmployeeDTO dto = new EmployeeDTO();
dto.setId(employee.getId());
dto.setName(employee.getName());
dto.setEmail(employee.getEmail());

2) Automatic Mapping (ModelMapper)

Java
ModelMapper mapper = new ModelMapper();
EmployeeDTO dto = mapper.map(employee, EmployeeDTO.class);
FeatureManual MappingAutomatic Mapping
Code amountMore codeLess code
ControlBetter controlFaster development
Library neededNoneModelMapper / MapStruct
Best forSmall projectsLarge enterprise projects

Customizing JSON Serialization

Serialization = Java Object → JSON. Use these annotations to control exactly what gets serialized:

AnnotationPurpose
@JsonIgnoreExclude a field from JSON output
@JsonPropertyRename a field in JSON output
@JsonIncludeIgnore null values
@JsonFormatFormat date/time values
@JsonCreatorSpecify constructor for deserialization
Java — Example
public class EmployeeDTO {
    private Long id;
    private String name;

    @JsonIgnore
    private String password;  // Not included in JSON

    @JsonProperty("email_address")
    private String email;      // Renamed in JSON
}

API Versioning

API Versioning = maintaining multiple versions of the same API without breaking existing clients.

⚠️ Without Versioning
Old mobile app expects: {id, name}
New API returns: {id, name, email, department}

Old app may break. Solution: Version your APIs.
StrategyExampleNotes
URI Versioning/api/v1/employeesMost common ✅
Request Param/employees?version=1Simple but messy URLs
Header VersioningAPI-Version: 1Clean URLs, harder to test
Media TypeAccept: application/vnd.company.v1+jsonEnterprise grade

Backward Compatibility

Backward Compatibility = old clients continue working even after the API is updated.

💡 Why Important
Companies cannot force millions of users to update their apps immediately. Old apps and new apps must work together simultaneously.

Advantages

Hides sensitive data from clients Reduces response payload size Decouples API from database design Supports API versioning Enables backward compatibility Improves API security Easier enterprise API maintenance

RESTful CRUD Operations

How the four fundamental data operations — Create, Read, Update, Delete — map to HTTP methods in a REST API, plus input validation and optimistic locking for concurrent safety.

CRUD ↔ HTTP Mapping

CRUDHTTP MethodPurposeExample URI
CreatePOSTInsert new resourcePOST /api/users
ReadGETRetrieve resourceGET /api/users/123
UpdatePUT / PATCHModify resourcePUT /api/users/123
DeleteDELETERemove resourceDELETE /api/users/123

Real-World CRUD Examples

ApplicationCreateReadUpdateDelete
InstagramCreate PostRead FeedUpdate CaptionDelete Post
AmazonAdd ProductView ProductUpdate PriceDelete Product
BankingCreate AccountView BalanceUpdate DetailsClose Account

HTTP Methods for CRUD

🟢 A) CREATE — POST
Creates a new resource in the database.

POST /api/users → Creates a new user
🔵 B) READ — GET
Retrieves data from the database.

GET /api/users → All users
GET /api/users/123 → User with ID 123
🟡 C) UPDATE — PUT / PATCH
Modifies existing data.

PUT /api/users/123 → Replace entire user object
PATCH /api/users/123 → Partially update (e.g. only email)
🔴 D) DELETE — DELETE
Removes data from the database.

DELETE /api/users/123 → Deletes user with ID 123

Validating Input Data — Bean Validation

Validation ensures incoming client data is correct, complete, and follows business rules before it reaches the database.

⚠️ Without Validation
Client sends: {name: "", age: -5, email: "abc"} → Invalid data reaches database.
AnnotationDescriptionExample
@NotNullValue cannot be nullMandatory field
@NotBlankCannot be null or blankUsername
@NotEmptyCannot be emptyCollections / Strings
@Size(min, max)Length constraint@Size(min=8) → password
@Min(value)Minimum numeric value@Min(18) → age
@Max(value)Maximum numeric value@Max(100) → marks
@EmailValid email formatUser email address
@PatternRegular expressionPhone / PAN number
@PositiveMust be positivePrice, quantity
@PastDate must be in pastDate of birth
@FutureDate must be futureAppointment booking
@ValidTriggers validation on object@Valid @RequestBody

Complete Validation Example

Java — EmployeeDTO.java
public class EmployeeDTO {

    @NotBlank          // Name cannot be blank
    private String name;

    @Email             // Must be a valid email
    private String email;

    @Min(18)           // Minimum age is 18
    private int age;
}
Java — Controller using @Valid
@PostMapping("/employees")
public Employee createEmployee(
        @Valid                    // Triggers validation
        @RequestBody EmployeeDTO dto) {
    return service.save(dto);
}

Optimistic Locking for Concurrent Updates

Optimistic Locking prevents users from accidentally overwriting each other's updates — the Lost Update Problem.

Lost Update Problem — Without Locking
Database: Salary = 50000

User A reads → User B reads → User A updates to 60000 → User B updates to 55000

Final DB: 55000 — User A's change is LOST.
✅ Solution — @Version
Every record has a version number. When User B tries to update using old Version 1 (after User A already changed it to Version 2), JPA rejects the update and throws OptimisticLockException.
Java — @Version on Entity
@Entity
public class Employee {

    @Id
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    @Version             // Automatically managed by JPA
    private Long version;
}
FeatureOptimistic LockingPessimistic Locking
AssumptionConflicts are rareConflicts are common
DB lock while reading❌ No lock✅ Locks immediately
PerformanceBetterLower concurrency
MechanismVersion numbersDatabase locks
Preferred forWeb applicationsHigh-contention systems

Advantages

Standardized CRUD via HTTP Strong input validation improves data integrity Optimistic locking prevents lost updates Better scalability and concurrency Enterprise-ready architecture Easier maintenance and testing
Module 7 · Spring REST · 7f

RESTful HATEOAS

HATEOAS makes your API self-navigating — instead of returning just data, the server also returns hyperlinks telling the client exactly what actions it can perform next.

The Problem — How Does the Client Know What to Do Next?

Traditional REST Response
{"id":101, "name":"Vishal", "email":"v@gmail.com"}

Now the client wants to: Update Employee · Delete Employee · View All Employees

How does it know which URL to call? Usually from hardcoded documentation.
If an endpoint changes → client breaks.

HATEOAS solves this — the server tells the client what to do next.

What is HATEOAS?

  • HATEOAS stands for Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State.
  • A REST principle where the server includes hyperlinks inside the response so clients can discover available actions dynamically.
  • Instead of only data, the server sends: Data + Related Links + Possible Next Actions.

Real-Life Analogy — Shopping Mall

Shopping Mall Navigation Signs
When you enter a mall, you see:
← Food Court  → Parking  ↑ Cinema  ↓ Exit

You don't need to ask anyone. The mall provides navigation automatically.

HATEOAS provides the same navigation inside API responses.

Traditional REST vs HATEOAS

📄

Traditional REST

JSON Response
{
  "id": 101,
  "name": "Vishal"
}

Client must know all URLs in advance. Hardcoded. Breaks on change.

🔗

HATEOAS Response

JSON with Links
{
  "id": 101,
  "name": "Vishal",
  "_links": {
    "self": "/employees/101",
    "update": "/employees/101",
    "delete": "/employees/101",
    "all": "/employees"
  }
}

Client follows links. Self-documenting. Resilient to change.

Hypermedia Components

ComponentPurpose
ResourceActual data (Employee, Product, etc.)
LinkURL pointing to an action or resource
Relation (rel)The meaning/label of the link
HTTP MethodWhat action to perform on the link
RepresentationJSON / XML format of the response

Common Link Relations (rel)

RelationMeaning
selfCurrent resource URL
nextNext resource / page
prevPrevious resource / page
updateUpdate this resource
deleteDelete this resource
collectionEntire collection of resources

Spring HATEOAS — Main Classes

ClassPurposeExample
EntityModel<T>Wraps one resource with linksEntityModel<Employee>
CollectionModel<T>Wraps multiple resources with linksCollectionModel<Employee>
RepresentationModel<T>Base model for all hypermediaExtend for custom models
LinkRepresents a single hyperlinkLink.of("/employees/1")

Basic EntityModel Example

Java — Simple EntityModel
@RestController
public class EmployeeController {

    @GetMapping("/employees/{id}")
    public EntityModel<Employee> getEmployee(@PathVariable Long id) {

        Employee employee = new Employee(id, "Vishal");

        // Wrap employee inside EntityModel
        EntityModel<Employee> model = EntityModel.of(employee);

        return model;
    }
}

Adding Hyperlinks to Response

Java — EntityModel with Links
@GetMapping("/employees/{id}")
public EntityModel<Employee> getEmployee(@PathVariable Long id) {

    Employee employee = new Employee(id, "Vishal");

    EntityModel<Employee> model = EntityModel.of(employee);

    // Add self link
    model.add(Link.of("/employees/" + id).withSelfRel());

    // Add allEmployees link
    model.add(Link.of("/employees").withRel("allEmployees"));

    return model;
}
JSON — Response with Links
{
  "id": 101,
  "name": "Vishal",
  "_links": {
    "self": { "href": "/employees/101" },
    "allEmployees": { "href": "/employees" }
  }
}

Consuming a HATEOAS API

A client reads the links from the response instead of hardcoding URLs:

Server returns response with _links.update.href = "/employees/101"
↓
Client reads the update link from response
↓
Client calls PUT /employees/101 — no URL hardcoded
↓
If URL changes, only server response changes — client still works

Advantages

Self-discoverable APIs Reduced dependency on documentation Easier API evolution Better client-server decoupling Dynamic navigation REST Maturity Level 3 (Richardson Model)

Disadvantages

⚠️ Trade-offs
Larger response size · More complex implementation · Not required for every REST API · Many public APIs choose simpler REST without HATEOAS.
Module 7 · Spring REST · 7g

Content Negotiation and Media Types

One API — multiple formats. Content Negotiation lets the client choose whether it wants JSON, XML, or a custom format, without the server needing separate endpoints for each.

The Problem — Multiple Clients, Multiple Formats

One API serving many clients
React Website wants JSON · Flutter App wants JSON · Banking Software wants XML · Legacy Java App wants XML

Without Content Negotiation:
GET /employees/json — separate endpoint for JSON
GET /employees/xml — separate endpoint for XML

Very bad design.

With Content Negotiation:
GET /employees — one endpoint, client chooses format.

What is Content Negotiation?

  • Content Negotiation is the process by which the client and server agree on the format of the request and response data.
  • The client says: "I want the response in this format." The server checks if it supports it → sends it or returns an error.

Restaurant Analogy

Tea or Coffee?
The waiter asks: "Would you like tea or coffee?"
You choose. The waiter serves only what you asked for.

Similarly, the client chooses: JSON · XML · PDF · Custom Media Type
The server sends exactly the requested format.

What are Media Types?

A Media Type (also called MIME Type) tells the client what type of content is being sent in the response.

Media TypeDescription
application/jsonJSON data
application/xmlXML data
text/plainPlain text
text/htmlHTML content
image/pngPNG image
image/jpegJPEG image
application/pdfPDF document
ℹ️ Why Media Types?
Without a media type, the browser/client cannot know whether the response is JSON, XML, PDF, or an image. The Content-Type header carries the media type and makes everything clear.

The Accept Header

The Accept header is sent by the client in the HTTP request to tell the server which format it prefers.

HTTP Request Headers
# Client wants JSON
Accept: application/json

# Client wants XML
Accept: application/xml
cURL Example
curl -H "Accept: application/json" http://localhost:8080/employees

produces and consumes

📤

produces

Specifies what format this API will return in the response.

Java
@GetMapping(produces = "application/json")
📥

consumes

Specifies what format this API can receive in the request body.

Java
@PostMapping(consumes = "application/json")
AttributeDirectionPurposeExample
producesResponse (outgoing)Declares response format"application/json"
consumesRequest (incoming)Declares accepted input format"application/json"

Complete Example

Java — EmployeeController.java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/employees")
public class EmployeeController {

    @GetMapping(produces = "application/json")
    public Employee getEmployee() {
        return new Employee(101, "Vishal");
    }
}
✅ Response Header
Content-Type: application/json

The client now knows the response is JSON.

Content Negotiation Flow

Client sends request with Accept: application/xml
↓
Spring checks if controller supports application/xml in produces
↓
If supported → serialize response as XML · set Content-Type: application/xml
↓
If not supported → return 406 Not Acceptable

Producing Custom Media Types

You can define completely custom media types for versioned or specialized APIs:

Java — Custom Media Type
@GetMapping(
    value = "/employees",
    produces = {"application/vnd.company.employee-v1+json"}
)
public Employee getEmployee() {
    return new Employee(101, "Vishal");
}
ℹ️ Custom Media Type Convention
application/vnd.{company}.{resource}-v{version}+{format}

This is a common pattern for media type versioning — one of the four API versioning strategies.

Content Negotiation — Summary

ConceptHTTP HeaderDirectionPurpose
AcceptAccept: application/jsonRequest (client → server)Client declares preferred format
Content-TypeContent-Type: application/jsonResponse (server → client)Server declares actual format sent
producesSpring annotationController configFormats this endpoint can return
consumesSpring annotationController configFormats this endpoint can receive

Spring Boot Actuator for REST Monitoring

A production-ready dashboard for your running Spring Boot application — exposing health, metrics, beans, mappings, and more through dedicated HTTP endpoints.

The Problem — Production Without Monitoring

Production Nightmare
Your app is deployed. Thousands of users are active. Suddenly:

API becomes slow · Database connection fails · Server memory hits 95% · Application crashes

How will you know what happened? You can't manually check logs every minute.

You need a tool that tells you: Is the app running? How much memory? How many requests? Is DB connected?

This is exactly why Spring Boot Actuator exists.

What is Spring Boot Actuator?

  • Spring Boot Actuator is a production-ready monitoring and management module that exposes endpoints to monitor, manage, and inspect a running Spring Boot application.
  • It exposes: Application Health · Metrics · Environment · Beans · Mappings · Logging · Thread Info.

Car Dashboard Analogy

🚗

Car Dashboard

Fuel level · Speed · Engine Temperature · Oil pressure

📊

Actuator Dashboard

Memory usage · CPU · Application Health · Request count · Database status

Real-Life Analogy — Hospital

Doctor ChecksActuator Checks
Heart RateJVM Memory
Blood PressureCPU Usage
Oxygen LevelDatabase Health
TemperatureDisk Space

Adding Actuator — One Dependency

pom.xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
💡 Auto-Configured
Spring Boot automatically configures Actuator after this dependency is added. No additional setup needed to get started.

Common Actuator Endpoints

EndpointPurpose
/actuatorLists all available endpoints
/actuator/healthApplication health status

/actuator/envEnvironment properties

/actuator/loggersLogging configuration
/actuator/threaddumpThread information
/actuator/heapdumpJVM heap dump

/actuator/health

Checks whether the application is healthy. Most commonly used in production monitoring.

JSON — Response
{
  "status": "UP"
}
StatusMeaning
UPApplication is healthy

OUT_OF_SERVICEIn maintenance mode

/actuator/info

Displays custom application information — version, build date, description, etc.

JSON — Response

  "app": {

  }

Custom Metrics

A Metric is a measurable value representing the application's behavior or performance.

Metric TypePurposeExample
CounterCounts events (always increases)Login attempts, Orders placed

E-Commerce Custom Metrics Example
Orders per minute · Successful payments · Failed logins · User registrations

These are business-specific metrics that go beyond what Actuator tracks by default.

Securing Actuator Endpoints

⚠️ Security Risk — /actuator/env
Exposing /actuator/env may reveal: Database URL · Server Config · Environment Variables · Passwords

Only administrators should access sensitive endpoints.
Authentication Authorization Spring Security Role-based Access Control

Customizing Actuator Endpoints

application.properties
# Expose only health and info
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info

# Hide all endpoints
management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude=*

# Expose all endpoints (use with security!)
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*

# Change base path from /actuator to /manage
management.endpoints.web.base-path=/manage
ConfigurationEffect
include=health,infoOnly health and info are accessible
exclude=*All endpoints hidden
include=*All endpoints exposed (secure this!)

Enterprise Monitoring Integration

ℹ️ Prometheus & Grafana
Actuator metrics can be exported to Prometheus (metrics collection) and visualized in Grafana (dashboards). This is the standard monitoring stack in enterprise Spring Boot deployments.

Advantages

Production-ready monitoring Easy health checks Performance metrics Supports DevOps tools Quick issue diagnosis Integrates with Prometheus & Grafana

Disadvantages

Sensitive endpoints can expose internal information · Additional security configuration required · Some endpoints increase resource usage · Misconfiguration can create security risks.
Module 7 · Spring REST · 7i

Security and Authentication in RESTful APIs

Without security, anyone on the internet can view, modify, or delete your API data. Spring Security answers the two fundamental questions: Who are you? (Authentication) and What can you do? (Authorization).

The Problem — Unsecured API

⚠️ Without Security — Anyone Can:
View all employee data · Delete employees · Modify salaries · Create fake employees

We need to answer: Who are you? (Authentication) and What are you allowed to do? (Authorization)

What is Spring Security?

  • Spring Security is a powerful Spring Framework module that secures applications by providing: Authentication · Authorization · Password Encryption · Session Management · CSRF Protection · JWT Support · OAuth2 Support.

Security Guard Analogy

Company Security Guard
Before anyone enters the company:

Guard asks: "Who are you?" → Identity verified (Authentication)
Guard checks: "Which rooms can you enter?" → Access checked (Authorization)

Exactly how Spring Security works.

Spring Security Components

ComponentPurpose
Security Filter ChainIntercepts every incoming request
Authentication ManagerVerifies user identity
UserDetailsServiceLoads user information from DB
Password EncoderEncrypts and verifies passwords
Security ContextStores the authenticated user info

Authentication

Authentication = Verifying the identity of the user. Answers: "Who are you?"

MethodDescriptionUsed For
Username & PasswordMost common methodLogin forms
JWT TokenCompact secure tokenModern REST APIs
OAuth2Third-party loginGoogle · GitHub login
LDAPDirectory-based authEnterprise apps
API KeyKey-based accessMachine-to-Machine APIs

Authorization

Authorization = Checking what an authenticated user can do. Answers: "What can you access?"

👑

ADMIN Role

Can: View all · Create · Update · Delete

👤

EMPLOYEE Role

Can: View own data · Update own profile
Cannot: Delete

🛒

CUSTOMER Role

Can: View products · Place orders
Cannot: Access admin panel

Token-Based Authentication — JWT

  • JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, secure token used for authentication in REST APIs.
  • Instead of storing user sessions on the server, the server issues a token. The client sends this token with every request.
ℹ️ Why JWT for REST?
REST APIs are stateless — the server should not remember users between requests. JWT solves this by letting the client carry authentication info in a self-contained token.

JWT Login Flow

Client sends Username + Password
↓
Server authenticates credentials
↓
Server generates JWT token and returns it
↓
Client stores token (localStorage / memory)
↓
Every future request includes: Authorization: Bearer <token>
↓
Server verifies token → Access Granted

JWT Structure — 3 Parts

📋

1) Header

JSON
{
  "alg": "HS256",
  "typ": "JWT"
}

Token type + algorithm used

👤

2) Payload

JSON
{
  "username": "Vishal",
  "role": "ADMIN"
}

User info / claims

🔐

3) Signature

Verifies token authenticity.
Prevents tampering.
Created using a secret key.

Session vs JWT

FeatureSessionJWT
StorageServer stores sessionClient stores token
StateStatefulStateless
MemoryMore server memoryLess memory
Best forTraditional web appsREST APIs

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

  • CORS is a browser security mechanism that controls whether one website can access resources from another origin.
  • Origin = Protocol + Host + Port
CORS Example
Website A (http://localhost:3000) tries to call API B (http://localhost:8080)

The browser blocks this by default to prevent malicious sites from accessing your API.

Solution: Explicitly allow trusted origins using @CrossOrigin.
Java — @CrossOrigin
@CrossOrigin(origins = "http://localhost:3000")
@GetMapping("/employees")
public List<Employee> getAllEmployees() {
    return employeeService.getAllEmployees();
}

Advantages

Strong application security Stateless JWT auth for REST Fine-grained role-based access control Easy frontend integration Suitable for microservices Browser security via CORS

Disadvantages

⚠️ Trade-offs
Security configuration can be complex · JWT tokens must be protected on the client side · Incorrect CORS config may expose APIs · Token revocation requires additional strategies (blacklist / refresh tokens).

Testing RESTful APIs

How do you know your APIs work correctly — and keep working after future code changes? Automated testing with JUnit, Mockito, and MockMvc gives you confidence without manual checks.

Why Do We Need API Testing?

❌

Without Testing

Bugs reach production · Customers face errors · Future updates break existing APIs · Every change requires manual verification

✅

With Testing

Reliability · Stability · Maintainability · Automated verification on every change · Bugs caught early

Car Factory Analogy
Every car is tested before leaving the factory.

Similarly, every API should be tested before deployment.

What is API Testing?

API Testing verifies that REST APIs behave correctly by checking:

Functionality Inputs Outputs Status Codes Business Logic Error Handling

Types of Testing

TypePurposeExample
Unit TestingTest one component in isolationOnly EmployeeController
Integration TestingTest multiple components togetherController + Service + DB
System TestingTest complete applicationFull app end-to-end
End-to-End TestingSimulate real user behaviourBrowser-driven flow

Unit Testing REST Controllers

Unit Testing verifies a single class in isolation — no database, no external services.

ℹ️ Unit Test Scope
Only test EmployeeController — not the real database, not external services. Everything else is faked using Mockito.

JUnit — Java Testing Framework

  • JUnit is the most widely used Java testing framework — provides test execution, assertions, and test reports.
AnnotationPurpose
@TestMarks a method as a test case
@BeforeEachRuns before every test method
@AfterEachRuns after every test method
@BeforeAllRuns once before all tests in the class
@AfterAllRuns once after all tests in the class
Java — JUnit Example
@Test
void testGetEmployee() {
    // Verify getEmployee() returns expected value
}

Mockito — Mocking Framework

  • Mockito creates fake objects (Mocks) for dependencies, so tests don't need a real database or external service.
AnnotationPurpose
@MockCreate a mock (fake) object
@InjectMocksInject mocks into the class under test
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)Enable Mockito in JUnit 5
Java — Mockito Setup
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class EmployeeControllerTest {

    @Mock
    EmployeeService service;  // Fake service — no real DB

    @InjectMocks
    EmployeeController controller;  // Real controller under test
}

Integration Testing

Integration Testing verifies that multiple components work correctly together.

Controller
↓
Service
↓
Repository
↓
Database
⚠️ Why Integration Testing is Needed
Unit tests may all pass individually, but Controller + Database may still fail when combined. Integration Testing catches these cross-component issues.

MockMvc — Simulating HTTP Requests

  • MockMvc simulates HTTP requests without starting a real web server.
  • Instead of opening a browser and calling the API, MockMvc directly simulates GET, POST, PUT, DELETE inside the test.
Java — MockMvc Example
mockMvc.perform(get("/employees"))
       .andExpect(status().isOk())
       .andExpect(jsonPath("$[0].name").value("Vishal"));
ApproachWithout MockMvcWith MockMvc
Server needed✅ Start real server❌ No server needed
Browser needed✅ Open browser❌ Directly in test
SpeedSlowFast
AutomationManualAutomated

Test Coverage

Test Coverage measures how much of your application code is executed during testing.

ℹ️ Example
Application: 100 methods · Tests execute: 80 methods → Coverage: 80%

100% coverage is ideal but not always possible. Use JaCoCo to measure coverage automatically.
Coverage TypeWhat It Measures
Line CoverageHow many lines were executed
Method CoverageHow many methods were called
Branch Coverageif/else branches covered
Statement CoverageIndividual statements executed

Testing Best Practices

🔖 Write Independent Tests
Each test should work independently — no test should depend on another test's result.
🔖 Test One Thing Per Test
One test → one responsibility. Don't combine multiple assertions for different behaviours.
🔖 Use Meaningful Names
Bad: test1()    Good: shouldReturnEmployeeWhenIdExists()
🔖 Mock External Systems
Don't call real Payment Gateways, Email Servers, or third-party APIs during unit tests — use Mockito instead.
🔖 Test Both Positive and Negative Cases
Positive: Employee found → return data
Negative: Employee not found → return 404
🔖 Keep Tests Fast
Slow tests discourage frequent execution. Fast tests → developers run them often → better quality.

Documenting RESTful APIs

API documentation is the user manual for developers — Springdoc OpenAPI auto-generates it from your Spring annotations, and Swagger UI turns it into an interactive browser-based testing tool.

What is API Documentation?

  • API Documentation is a structured description of a REST API that explains available endpoints, HTTP methods, request parameters, request/response bodies, status codes, authentication, and examples.
  • It acts as a user manual for developers integrating with your API.

Analogy — Mobile Phone Manual

New Mobile Phone
Inside the box you find a manual explaining: How to switch it on · How to charge it · What each button does

API Documentation works the same way — it tells developers exactly how to use every endpoint.

What API Documentation Contains

InformationExample
Endpoint/employees
HTTP MethodGET
Parametersid
Request BodyEmployee JSON
ResponseEmployee JSON
Status Codes200 · 404
AuthenticationJWT Required

OpenAPI vs Swagger

📜

OpenAPI

An industry-standard specification for describing REST APIs — defines structure, endpoints, parameters, responses, and authentication.

OpenAPI = The Rules

🛠️

Swagger

A collection of tools that implement the OpenAPI specification — used to create, visualize, and test APIs.

Swagger = The Implementation Tool

ℹ️ Spring Boot 3 — Use Springdoc OpenAPI
Modern Spring Boot 3 applications use Springdoc OpenAPI (not the older Springfox/Swagger2). It automatically generates OpenAPI documentation from Spring annotations.

Documentation Annotations

AnnotationPurpose
@OperationDescribe what an API endpoint does
@ParameterDescribe a parameter
@SchemaDescribe a model/DTO
@ApiResponseDescribe a possible HTTP response
@ApiResponsesGroup multiple @ApiResponse
@TagGroup related APIs together

Complete Example

Java — EmployeeController.java with Docs
@RestController
@Tag(name = "Employee Management",
     description = "Endpoints for managing employees")
public class EmployeeController {

    @Operation(
        summary = "Get employee by ID",
        description = "Returns a single employee based on the provided ID"
    )
    @ApiResponses(value = {
        @ApiResponse(responseCode = "200", description = "Employee found"),
        @ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", description = "Employee not found")
    })
    @GetMapping("/employees/{id}")
    public Employee getEmployee(@PathVariable Long id) {
        // Implementation
    }

    @Operation(
        summary = "Create new employee",
        description = "Creates a new employee record"
    )
    @PostMapping("/employees")
    public Employee createEmployee(@RequestBody Employee employee) {
        // Implementation
    }
}

Swagger UI

Swagger UI is a web interface where developers can view APIs, read documentation, send test requests, and view responses — without needing Postman.

💡 Access Swagger UI
Open: http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui/index.html

You'll see all documented endpoints, parameters, request/response examples, and a "Try it out" button to test directly in the browser.

Auto-Generated Documentation Endpoints

URLContent
/v3/api-docsRaw OpenAPI JSON specification
/swagger-ui/index.htmlInteractive Swagger UI browser interface

Documentation Best Practices

🔖 Use Meaningful Endpoint Names
Bad: /getData    Good: /employees
🔖 Document All Status Codes
Always explain: 200 OK · 201 Created · 400 Bad Request · 404 Not Found · 500 Server Error
🔖 Include Request and Response Examples
Show real JSON examples so developers know exactly what to send and expect back.
🔖 Group Related APIs with @Tag
Employee APIs · Order APIs · Product APIs — grouping makes large APIs easier to navigate.
🔖 Keep Documentation Synchronized
Documentation must always match the actual implementation. Outdated docs are worse than no docs.

Advantages

Automatic documentation from annotations Interactive API testing in browser Reduces developer confusion Improves frontend-backend communication Saves integration development time Industry-standard OpenAPI format

Disadvantages

⚠️ Trade-offs
Documentation must stay synchronized with code · Publicly exposing Swagger UI in production may reveal API details · Sensitive endpoints should be secured or hidden in production.
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8a · i

What is SonarQube?

An automatic code reviewer that catches bugs, security holes, code smells, and duplication before they ever reach production — Grammarly for your Java code.

What is SonarQube?

  • SonarQube is an open-source code quality inspection tool that automatically analyzes source code and identifies issues such as:
Bugs Security Vulnerabilities Code Smells Duplicate Code High Complexity Low Test Coverage
  • It helps developers write clean, secure, maintainable, and reliable code.

Grammarly Analogy

SonarQube = Grammarly for Code
Suppose you wrote a Java program. It compiles. It runs. It gives the correct output.

Does that mean the code is perfect? No.

It may still have: unnecessary code · repeated code · security issues · poor naming · very complex methods · bad design.

Humans miss these during code reviews. SonarQube checks them automatically.

Why Do We Need SonarQube?

❌

Before SonarQube

Developers had to: review thousands of lines manually · search for bugs · verify coding standards · detect duplicate code · estimate quality

Time-consuming. Impractical at scale.

✅

With SonarQube

Automatic analysis on every build · Consistent standards enforced · Integrated into CI/CD pipelines · Reports generated instantly

Code Example — What SonarQube Detects

Java — Problematic Code
public void process() {
    int a = 10;      // Used
    int b = 20;      // ⚠️ Unused variable
    if (a > 5) {
        if (a > 8) {
            if (a > 9) {    // ⚠️ High nesting complexity
                System.out.println("Hello");
            }
        }
    }
}
⚠️ SonarQube Would Report
Unused variable b · High complexity due to nested if statements · Suggestion to simplify the method

The code still runs — but SonarQube highlights areas for improvement.

SonarQube Report — Sample Output

SonarQube Dashboard Report
Project Status
───────────────────────────
Bugs              :  2
Security Issues   :  1
Code Smells       :  15
Duplicated Code   :  4%
Coverage          :  82%
Quality Gate      :  ✅ Passed
ℹ️ Quality Gate
A Quality Gate is a set of conditions your code must meet before it can proceed to the next stage in the CI/CD pipeline. If conditions fail → pipeline blocked.

Benefits of SonarQube

BenefitExplanation
Detects BugsFinds programming mistakes before release
Improves SecurityIdentifies security vulnerabilities in code
Better MaintainabilityEncourages clean, readable code
Detects Duplicate CodeReduces copy-paste issues
Measures ComplexityHighlights code that is hard to understand
Team StandardsEnsures consistent coding practices across the team
Saves Review TimeAutomates many manual review checks
CI/CD IntegrationAnalyzes code automatically during builds

Advantages

Improves software quality Finds bugs early in development Detects security vulnerabilities Promotes clean code practices Reduces maintenance costs Integrates with CI/CD pipelines Supports many programming languages Useful for teams of all sizes
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8a · ii

Static Code Analysis vs Runtime Testing

JUnit checks whether your code behaves correctly. SonarQube checks whether your code is written correctly. Both are needed — they solve completely different problems.

What is Static Code Analysis?

  • Static Code Analysis is the process of examining source code without executing it.
  • A tool like SonarQube reads your .java, .js, .py files and checks whether the code follows predefined quality rules.

What is Runtime Testing?

  • Runtime Testing means executing the application and observing whether it behaves correctly.
  • Examples: Unit Testing (JUnit) · Integration Testing · Functional Testing · Manual Testing.

Why Do We Need Both?

The Classic Question
"If I already have JUnit tests, why do I need SonarQube?"

Because they solve different problems.
Java — Same Code, Different Perspectives
public int divide(int a, int b) {
    return a / b;
}
✅

JUnit says: Test Passed

divide(10, 2) → output: 5

Behavior is correct.

⚠️

SonarQube still reports

Missing JavaDoc · Poor variable naming · Low test coverage · Code smell · Possible divide-by-zero risk

ℹ️ Key Insight
JUnit checks behavior. Does the method return the right result?
SonarQube checks code quality. Is the method written well?

Real-Life Analogy — Buying a Car

🔧

a) Static Inspection

Mechanic checks: Engine · Brakes · Tyres · Wiring · Oil

The car never moves.

This is Static Analysis.

🚗

b) Road Test

Mechanic drives the car. Checks: Speed · Braking · Steering · Engine performance

The car actually runs.

This is Runtime Testing.

Static Code Analysis vs Runtime Testing

FeatureStatic Code AnalysisRuntime Testing
When it runsWithout executing the codeWhile the program is running
ToolSonarQube · Checkstyle · PMDJUnit · Mockito · MockMvc
What it checksCode quality, style, security, smellsBehavior, outputs, business logic
CatchesUnused variables, complexity, duplicationWrong outputs, runtime exceptions
CI/CD stageAt code commit / buildDuring test execution phase
SpeedFast (no execution needed)Depends on test suite size

Advantages

Static Code Analysis

Finds problems before execution Improves maintainability Detects security issues early Encourages clean code Saves code review time Works well in CI/CD pipelines

Runtime Testing

Verifies actual program behavior Detects runtime exceptions Confirms business logic Validates outputs Ensures features work as expected
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8a · iii

SonarQube Architecture

SonarQube is built as a modular system — each component has a single responsibility, just like the departments of a company. Together they take raw source code and produce a quality report.

What is SonarQube Architecture?

  • SonarQube Architecture describes how its internal components work together to analyze source code and generate quality reports.
  • It consists of: Web Server · Compute Engine · Search Server (Elasticsearch) · Scanner · SonarQube Server · Database.

Company Analogy

SonarQube = A Company
A company has different departments: Reception · Employees · Records Department · Search Department

Similarly, SonarQube has different components — each performing one job.

Together they produce the final code quality report.

This follows the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) — each component has one primary responsibility.

The 6 Components

🔖 a) Web Server
Provides the SonarQube user interface that developers access through a browser.

Handles: User requests · API calls · Dashboard access
Built with: Spring Boot

Access via: http://localhost:9000
Shows: Dashboard · Issues · Metrics · Quality Gate · Reports
🔖 b) Compute Engine
The processing brain of SonarQube. After the Scanner uploads analysis data, the Compute Engine processes it.

Responsibilities: Process analysis reports · Calculate metrics · Apply quality rules · Determine Quality Gate status · Prepare final results

Without the Compute Engine, SonarQube cannot produce meaningful reports.
🔖 c) Search Server (Elasticsearch)
Provides fast searching and filtering of analysis results.

Imagine: 20 million lines of code · 50,000 issues → searching directly in the database would be slow.

Elasticsearch: Indexes reports · Enables very fast searching · Supports dashboard filters
🔖 d) SonarQube Scanner (Client)
The messenger — reads source code and sends analysis data to the SonarQube Server.

Runs on: Developer's machine or build server
Does NOT: Store reports or generate dashboards
Supports: Multiple languages and build tools (Maven, Gradle, etc.)
🔖 e) SonarQube Server
The central hub that stores configuration, manages users and permissions, and coordinates between all components.
🔖 f) Database
Stores all SonarQube information permanently.

Stores: Configuration settings · User information · Analysis results · Quality Gate status
Common databases: H2 (for testing) · PostgreSQL (for production)

Note: Source code is NOT stored — only metadata and analysis results.

Component Summary

ComponentRoleAnalogy
Web ServerUI / Browser interfaceReception desk
Compute EngineProcesses analysis reportsProcessing department
ElasticsearchFast search and indexingIndex/Search department
ScannerReads code and sends to serverMessenger / Field agent
SonarQube ServerCentral hub / coordinatorManagement office
DatabasePermanent data storageRecords department

How All Components Work Together

1. Developer runs SonarQube Scanner on local machine / CI server
↓
2. Scanner sends analysis data to the Web Server
↓
3. Web Server forwards the task to the Compute Engine
↓
4. Compute Engine analyzes the code and applies quality rules
↓
5. Results are stored in the Database
↓
6. Elasticsearch indexes the data for fast searching
↓
7. Users access the Dashboard via the Web Server

Advantages

Modular architecture — easy to maintain Easy to scale individual components Faster searching with Elasticsearch Efficient background processing via Compute Engine Clear separation of responsibilities (SRP) Supports enterprise-sized projects
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8a · iv

Quality Profiles and Quality Gates

A Quality Profile is the rulebook SonarQube checks code against during analysis. A Quality Gate is the pass/fail decision made after analysis, based on the results.

What is a Quality Profile?

  • A Quality Profile is a collection of coding rules that SonarQube uses to analyze source code.
  • It tells SonarQube: "These are the rules you should check while analyzing my code."
  • Quality Profile = Rules to check code.

Why Do We Need a Quality Profile?

ℹ️ Different Organizations, Different Standards
Different organizations follow different coding standards — SonarQube allows each one to define its own custom rule set instead of applying the same rules to everyone.
OrganizationRequirement
Company AEvery public method must have comments
Company BComments not enforced, but strict security rules required

Example Quality Profile Rules

🔤

Naming

Variable names must be meaningful

🧹

Cleanliness

No unused variables

🧬

Duplication

Avoid duplicate code

📏

Method Size

Maximum method length = 50 lines

Together, rules like these form a Quality Profile.

Exam Marking Scheme Analogy

Quality Profile = Exam Marking Scheme
Before checking answer sheets, a teacher prepares a marking scheme.

The marking scheme tells the teacher: What is correct · What is wrong · How many marks to deduct

That marking scheme is exactly like a Quality Profile — it defines what to check, before the checking even begins.

What is a Quality Gate?

  • A Quality Gate is a set of conditions that determines whether the analyzed project passes or fails the quality check.
  • Quality Gate = Pass or Fail decision.

Why Do We Need a Quality Gate?

⚠️ Should This Still Be Deployed?
Imagine SonarQube finds: 100 Bugs · 50 Security Issues · 200 Code Smells

Should the project still be deployed? Maybe not.

A Quality Gate decides whether the project meets the minimum quality standard required before release.

Example Quality Gate Conditions

ConditionRequired Value
Bugs= 0
Security Vulnerabilities= 0
Code Coverage≥ 80%
Duplicated Code< 3%
All conditions met → Quality Gate Passed Any condition fails → Quality Gate Failed

Quality Profile vs Quality Gate

Quality ProfileQuality Gate
Collection of rulesCollection of conditions
Used during code analysisUsed after analysis
Decides what to checkDecides whether to pass or fail
Example: "No unused variables"Example: "No bugs allowed"

Worked Example

Quality Profile checks: No unused variables · No duplicate code · Method length < 50 lines · Naming conventions followed
↓
Analysis results: Bugs = 1 · Coverage = 85% · Duplicated Code = 2%
↓
Quality Gate evaluates: Bugs must be 0 ✗ · Coverage ≥ 80% ✓ · Duplicated Code < 3% ✓
↓
Final Result: QUALITY GATE FAILED
💡 Key Takeaway
Even though most conditions passed, one failed condition is enough to fail the Quality Gate. A Quality Profile decides what gets checked; a Quality Gate decides whether the project is good enough to ship.
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8b · i

Adding SonarQube Maven Plugin to pom.xml

Maven doesn't know what SonarQube is by default. The SonarQube Maven Plugin is the bridge that lets Maven send your project's code to the SonarQube Server for analysis.

What is a Maven Plugin?

  • A Maven Plugin is a software component that adds extra functionality to Maven.
  • By default, Maven knows how to: Compile Java code · Download dependencies · Run tests · Package the application (JAR/WAR).
  • If we want Maven to perform additional tasks, we add plugins.
PluginPurpose
Compiler PluginCompiles Java code
Surefire PluginRuns JUnit tests
Spring Boot PluginRuns Spring Boot applications
SonarQube Maven PluginPerforms code analysis

What is the SonarQube Maven Plugin?

ℹ️ Bridge Between Maven and SonarQube
The SonarQube Maven Plugin allows Maven to communicate with the SonarQube Server and send your project's code for analysis.

Without this plugin, Maven has no idea what SonarQube is.

Why Do We Need It?

Suppose you have a Spring Boot project and run mvn clean install. What does Maven actually do?

Project
↓
Compile
↓
Run Tests
↓
Create JAR
↓
Finish
⚠️ Notice Something?
No code quality analysis anywhere in that lifecycle.

Because Maven only knows its own lifecycle — it doesn't know: What SonarQube is · Where the SonarQube Server is · How to send analysis data.

So we install the SonarQube Maven Plugin.

Maven's Workflow — With the Sonar Plugin

Project
↓
Compile
↓
Run Tests
↓
Analyze Code (Sonar Plugin)
↓
Send Report to SonarQube
↓
Finish

Real-Life Analogy

Sonar Maven Plugin = Courier Service
Imagine you want to send a parcel. You have: a Parcel · a Destination — but no courier.

The parcel cannot reach the destination without one.

Now you use a courier service — this is exactly what the SonarQube Maven Plugin does: it carries your code's analysis data from Maven to the SonarQube Server.

Implementation

We add the plugin in the project's pom.xml.

pom.xml
<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.sonarsource.scanner.maven</groupId>
            <artifactId>sonar-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

Understanding the Tags

TagPurpose
<build>Contains build configuration
<plugins>Holds all Maven plugins
<plugin>Defines one plugin
<groupId>Organization providing the plugin
<artifactId>Name of the plugin

Advantages

Enables Maven to work with SonarQube Automates code analysis Fits naturally into the Maven build lifecycle Supports CI/CD pipelines Eliminates the need for manual code uploads
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8b · ii

Configuring sonar.host.url and Proxy Settings

Installing the Sonar Maven Plugin tells Maven how to analyze — sonar.host.url tells it where to send the report. Proxy settings control how that request travels through a corporate network.

What is sonar.host.url?

  • sonar.host.url is a configuration property that tells the SonarQube Maven Plugin where the SonarQube Server is running.
  • sonar.host.url = Address of the SonarQube Server.
  • Think of it as the destination address where Maven should send the analysis results.

Why Do We Need It?

⚠️ One Question Remains
You've installed the SonarQube Maven Plugin — Maven now knows how to perform SonarQube analysis.

But: "Where should I send the analysis report?"

Without a server address, Maven has no destination. So we configure:
sonar.host.url=http://localhost:9000

Now Maven knows exactly where to send the analysis.

Local vs Enterprise Server

🔖 1) Local Development
When SonarQube is installed on your own computer:
sonar.host.url=http://localhost:9000

localhost → Your own machine · 9000 → Default SonarQube port
🔖 2) Enterprise Environment
Companies usually have a centralized SonarQube server.

Example: sonar.host.url=http://sonarqube.company.com:9000

Every developer sends reports to the same server — this lets managers and teams monitor code quality for all projects in one place.

Implementation

application.properties
sonar.host.url=http://localhost:9000

Understanding the Parts

PropertyMeaning
sonar.host.urlSonarQube Server address
http://Communication protocol
localhostLocal machine
9000Default SonarQube port
💡 Remember
You don't need to memorize the exact syntax — just remember its purpose: it's the destination address for the analysis report.

What are Proxy Settings?

  • A Proxy Server is an intermediate server between your computer and another server.
Without Proxy: Computer → SonarQube Server
Computer
↓
Proxy Server
↓
SonarQube Server

Why Do Companies Use a Proxy?

ℹ️ Security First
Large organizations often block direct internet or network access for security reasons. A proxy helps: Monitor traffic · Improve security · Control access · Log requests.

Real-Life Analogy

Proxy = Class Monitor
Without Proxy: You → Teacher (direct)

With Proxy: You → Class Monitor → Teacher

The class monitor forwards your message to the teacher. Similarly, a proxy forwards network requests on your behalf.

Advantages

🎯

sonar.host.url

Identifies the SonarQube Server · Enables Maven ↔ SonarQube communication · Supports local and remote servers

🛡️

Proxy

Improves security · Controls network access · Required in some corporate environments

Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8b · iii

Running Maven Sonar Goals

One command ties everything together — cleans the project, verifies it builds and passes tests, then sends it to SonarQube for analysis.

Running Maven Sonar Goals

terminal
mvn clean verify sonar:sonar
CommandPurpose
mvnStarts Maven
cleanRemoves old build files
verifyCompiles and tests the project
sonar:sonarRuns SonarQube analysis
ℹ️ Three Tasks in Sequence
clean → Remove old build files.
verify → Build the project and run tests.
sonar:sonar → Analyze the code using SonarQube.

mvn clean verify sonar:sonar is a Maven command that cleans the project, verifies it, and then sends it to SonarQube for code quality analysis.

Why Do We Use All Three Together?

Submitting an Assignment
Imagine you are submitting an assignment to your teacher. Would you submit an old version, without checking mistakes? No.

You would: Throw away the old copy · Check the assignment · Submit the final version

The Maven command follows the same idea — clean, verify, then submit for analysis.

Goal 1 — clean

  • clean removes the previous build files, usually stored inside the target/ folder.
⚠️ Why Is It Needed?
Suppose yesterday you built your project. Today you modified some code.

If old compiled files remain, they may cause confusion or unexpected behavior — so Maven starts with a clean state.
Before → mvn clean → After
Project                    Project
 ├── src                    ├── src
 ├── pom.xml     mvn clean   └── pom.xml
 └── target (old) ────────►

Goal 2 — verify

  • verify checks whether the project is valid.
  • It performs: Compile the source code · Run unit tests · Verify the project can be built successfully.
  • If something fails here, SonarQube analysis should not continue.
🔖 Why?
Imagine your project doesn't even compile. There is no point analyzing its code quality before fixing the compilation errors first.

Goal 3 — sonar:sonar

  • This goal starts the SonarQube analysis.
  • It tells the SonarQube Maven Plugin: "Analyze this project and send the results to the SonarQube Server."
Plugin reads source code
↓
Plugin collects project information
↓
Plugin sends data to the SonarQube Server
↓
Compute Engine processes the analysis and generates the report

Advantages

Ensures a fresh build Prevents analysis of outdated files Verifies the project before analysis Automates code quality checks Integrates easily with CI/CD
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8b · iv

Project Tokens, Dashboard & Sonar Logs

A Project Token authenticates the build before analysis, the Dashboard shows results after analysis, and Sonar Logs tell you what happened during analysis.

What is a Project Token?

  • A Project Token is a unique secret key generated by SonarQube to authenticate a project or build tool.
  • Project Token = Password for your project (not for the user).
  • Instead of using your username and password every time, SonarQube allows you to use a secure token.
⚠️ Why Do We Need a Project Token?
Imagine anyone could send reports to your SonarQube Server. Someone could: Upload fake reports · Modify project data · Access analysis results.

To prevent this, SonarQube verifies that the request comes from an authorized source — that's why a Project Token is required.

Steps to Generate a Project Token

1. Log in to the SonarQube Dashboard
↓
2. Click on your profile icon (top-right corner)
↓
3. Select "My Account"
↓
4. Go to "Security" tab
↓
5. Under "Project Tokens", click "Generate"
↓
6. Enter a token name (e.g., "maven-project-token")
↓
7. Click "Generate"
↓
8. Copy the token value — you won't see it again

Using the Token

terminal
mvn clean verify sonar:sonar -Dsonar.login=your_project_token_here

Why Use a Project Token?

Security — tokens are more secure than passwords Reuse — same token for multiple builds Clean Access — revoke anytime without affecting user accounts

Viewing Scan Results on the Dashboard

After the analysis completes, SonarQube displays a dashboard containing the project's quality metrics.

MetricValue
ProjectBanking Application
Quality GatePASSED
Bugs2
Security1
Code Smells12
Coverage84%
Duplicated Code3%
🔖 1) Quality Gate
Overall project status — Passed or Failed.
🔖 2) Bugs
Programming errors that may cause incorrect behavior.
Java
String name = null;
System.out.println(name.length()); // Possible NullPointerException
🔖 3) Vulnerabilities
Security-related issues.
Java
String query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + input; // Possible SQL Injection
🔖 4) Code Smells
Poor coding practices — Long methods · Unused variables · Duplicate code · Poor naming.
🔖 5) Coverage
Shows how much of the code is tested. Example: Coverage = 85% means approximately 85% of the code is executed by unit tests.
🔖 6) Duplicated Code
Shows how much code has been copied. Lower duplication means better maintainability.

Interpreting Sonar Logs

  • When Maven runs SonarQube, messages appear in the terminal — these are called Sonar Logs.
  • Logs tell you: What is happening · Whether analysis succeeded · If any errors occurred.

Successful Log

terminal
INFO Scanner started
INFO Analyzing project
INFO Uploading report
INFO Quality Gate passed
BUILD SUCCESS
LogMeaning
Scanner startedAnalysis has begun
Analyzing projectSource code is being checked
Uploading reportResults are sent to the server
Quality Gate passedProject met quality conditions
BUILD SUCCESSEntire process completed successfully

Failed Log

terminal
ERROR Unable to connect to SonarQube Server
⚠️ Possible Reasons
SonarQube Server is not running · Wrong sonar.host.url · Network issue.

Comparison

Project TokenDashboardSonar Logs
Authenticates the projectDisplays analysis resultsShows execution details and errors
Used before analysisUsed after analysisUsed during analysis
