Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8c · i

Finding Duplicate Code

The same logic written in multiple places means the same bug has to be fixed in multiple places. SonarQube flags duplicate code because it multiplies maintenance effort and risk.

What is Duplicate Code?

  • Duplicate Code means the same or very similar code is written in multiple places within a project.
  • Instead of writing the logic once and reusing it, developers copy and paste the same code.

Why Do Developers Create Duplicate Code?

  • They want a quick solution.
  • Copy-paste is easier than creating a reusable method.
  • They don't know about code reusability.
  • Large teams accidentally implement the same logic in different classes.

Initially, it seems faster — but later it becomes difficult to maintain.

Why is Duplicate Code a Problem?

⚠️ One Bug, Ten Fixes
Imagine the same code is copied into 10 different files. Now suppose there is a bug in that code.

You must fix it 10 times instead of just once.

This increases: Maintenance effort · Chances of missing one copy · Bugs · Development time.

This is why SonarQube reports duplicate code.

Enterprise Example

E-Commerce Discount Calculation
Suppose an e-commerce application calculates discounts. Instead of writing discount calculation separately in the Order Service, Cart Service, and Checkout Service...

the company creates a single DiscountService that every module calls.
One implementation Easy maintenance Fewer bugs

How to Reduce Duplicate Code?

🧩

Reusable Methods

Extract shared logic into one method

🛠️

Utility Classes

Create helper/utility classes

🌳

Inheritance

Share behavior via a parent class, when appropriate

🧱

Composition

Build behavior by combining smaller objects

DRY Principle

💡 DRY = Don't Repeat Yourself
One of the most important software engineering principles.

Every piece of knowledge or logic should have one authoritative implementation.

Advantages of Removing Duplicate Code

Easier maintenance Less code to manage Fewer bugs Better readability Faster updates Improved code quality Better SonarQube score
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8c · ii

Cyclomatic Complexity

A software metric that counts the linearly independent paths through your code — the more decision points, the higher the complexity, and the harder the code is to understand, test, and maintain.

What is Cyclomatic Complexity?

  • Cyclomatic Complexity is a software metric used to indicate the number of linearly independent paths through a program's source code.
  • It tells us how difficult a piece of code is to understand, test, and maintain.
  • The more decision points your code has, the higher the complexity.

How is Cyclomatic Complexity Measured?

The basic idea is simple — every decision point increases complexity.

StatementIncreases Complexity?
ifYes
else ifYes
forYes
whileYes
do-whileYes
switchYes
catchYes
Simple statementNo
🔖 Graph Formula
Graphically, it's calculated as: V(G) = E − N + 2P

Where: E = Number of edges · N = Number of nodes · P = Number of connected components

Example

Java
public void exampleMethod() {
    if (condition1) {                       // +1
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {     // +1
            if (condition2) {                   // +1
                doSomething();
            }
        }
    } else if (condition3) {                // +1
        while (condition4) {                    // +1
            doSomethingElse();
        }
    }
}
💡 Total Complexity = 5
Base complexity of 1, plus one for each of the 4 decision points (if, for, nested if, else if, while).

Thresholds

LevelRange
Low1 – 10
Medium11 – 20
High21 – 50
Very High50+
ℹ️ What is a Threshold?
A Threshold is the maximum acceptable limit. For Cyclomatic Complexity, it tells us: "Beyond this value, the code is becoming too complex."

Why Do We Need Cyclomatic Complexity?

✅

Method A — 20 lines

No if · No loops · Easy to understand

⚠️

Method B — 20 lines

5 if · 2 for · 3 switch · 2 while

Even though both have 20 lines, Method B is much harder to Read · Debug · Test · Modify. That's why companies measure complexity.

⚠️ A High Cyclomatic Complexity Indicates
Harder to test · Harder to maintain · More prone to bugs · Difficult to understand

SonarQube Flagging

SonarQube sets thresholds to flag methods with high complexity.

Java
public void complexMethod() {
    if (a > 0) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
            if (i % 2 == 0) {
                System.out.println(i);
            }
        }
    }
}

This method has multiple nested conditions and loops, leading to high complexity. SonarQube will flag this and suggest simplification.

How to Reduce Complexity

Break down large methods Remove unnecessary nesting Use early returns Extract logic into smaller methods

Advantages of Measuring Complexity

Improves maintainability Easier testing Better readability Reduces bugs Encourages cleaner design Helps identify methods that should be refactored
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8c · iii

Spaghetti Design & Code Smells

A Code Smell is not a bug — the code works today, but its design suggests it will become difficult to modify, understand, or extend tomorrow.

What is a Code Smell?

  • A Code Smell is not a bug — it is a warning sign that indicates the code is poorly designed or difficult to maintain.
  • The code may work correctly today, but its design suggests it could become difficult to modify, understand, or extend in the future.
  • Code Smell = Code that works, but is written in a poor way.

What is Spaghetti Code (Spaghetti Design)?

  • Spaghetti Code is code that has become so tangled and disorganized that it is difficult to understand or modify.
  • It contains: Deeply nested if-else · Long methods · Large classes · Repeated code · Poor variable names · Mixed responsibilities.
  • It resembles a plate of spaghetti — everything is tangled together.

Why Do We Need to Identify Code Smells?

✅

Method A — calculateTax()

15 lines · Easy to understand

🍝

Method B — processEverything()

800 lines · Login, Payment, Database, Email, Validation, Report generation — all inside one method

Which one is easier to maintain? Obviously, Method A. SonarQube identifies methods like Method B as Code Smells.

Real-Life Analogy

Clean Room vs Messy Room
a) Clean Room — Everything has its place. Easy to find things.

b) Messy Room — Clothes, books, laptop, shoes — everything scattered. Finding anything becomes difficult.

The room still works. But it's poorly organized. That is exactly what a Code Smell is.

Example

Smelly Code

Java
public void process(){
    int a=10;
    int b=20;
    if(a>5){
        if(b>15){
            if(a<b){
                System.out.println("Done");
            }
        }
    }
}
⚠️ Problems
Poor variable names · Deep nesting

The program works. But the design is poor.

Better Version

Java
public void process(){
    int age = 10;
    int marks = 20;
    if(age > 5 && marks > 15 && age < marks){
        System.out.println("Done");
    }
}
💡 Much Easier to Read
Meaningful variable names (age, marks) plus a single flattened condition instead of three nested if blocks.

How to Remove Code Smells?

Break large methods into smaller ones Use meaningful variable names Remove unused code Remove duplicate code Reduce nesting Follow SOLID principles Refactor regularly

Advantages of Removing Code Smells

Easier maintenance Better readability Easier debugging Easier testing Better teamwork Higher code quality Better SonarQube report
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8c · iv

Lack of Unit Tests — Coverage Metrics

Coverage tells you what percentage of your code has actually been exercised by tests — the untested remainder is where hidden bugs like to hide.

What is Unit Test Coverage?

  • Unit Test Coverage (Code Coverage) is a metric that tells us how much of our source code is executed when unit tests run.
  • Coverage = Percentage of code tested by unit tests.
🔖 Worked Example
Suppose your application contains 100 lines of code.
Your JUnit tests execute 80 of those lines.

Then: Coverage = 80%

This means 80% of your code has been tested, while 20% has never been executed by the tests.

Why Do We Need Coverage?

Building a Car
Imagine you build a car. You test: Engine · Brakes · Steering

Would you confidently sell the car? No — the same idea applies to software.
⚠️ If Large Parts of Your Code Are Never Tested
Hidden bugs may exist · Changes can break functionality without being noticed · Developers have less confidence in the code.

That's why companies measure coverage.

Why Does SonarQube Check Coverage?

ℹ️ SonarQube Doesn't Run Tests Itself
SonarQube itself does not run unit tests. Instead:
JUnit (or another testing framework) runs the tests
↓
A coverage tool (such as JaCoCo) measures which lines were executed
↓
SonarQube reads the coverage report and displays it

How is Coverage Measured?

formula
Coverage (%) = (Tested Code / Total Code) × 100

Advantages

Improves confidence in the code Helps identify untested areas Encourages writing unit tests Reduces the risk of regressions Improves overall software quality
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8c · v

Improper Coding Standards

Code that compiles isn't automatically code that's readable. Coding standards are the shared grammar that keeps a hundred developers writing code the team can actually understand.

What are Coding Standards?

  • Coding Standards are a set of rules and best practices that developers follow while writing code to make it: Easy to read · Easy to understand · Easy to maintain · Consistent across the team.
  • Coding Standards = Rules for writing clean and consistent code.

Real-Life Analogy

Coding Standards = Grammar Rules
Think of coding standards as grammar rules for programming — they don't change what you can say, just how consistently understandable it is when you say it.

Why Do We Need Coding Standards?

Imagine a project with 100 developers. If everyone writes code in their own style:

DeveloperVariable Declaration
Developer Aint a;
Developer Bint studentAge;
Developer Cint x123;
💡 All Three Compile — Only One Is Clear
Although all three compile, which one is easiest to understand? studentAge.

Coding standards ensure everyone writes code in a similar and understandable way.

Why Does SonarQube Check Coding Standards?

⚠️ Poorly Written Code Is
Hard to understand · Hard to debug · Hard to maintain · More likely to introduce mistakes

Enforcing coding standards helps maintain a consistent codebase, especially in large teams.

Advantages

Improves readability Makes maintenance easier Reduces misunderstandings Encourages consistency Simplifies code reviews Improves overall code quality
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8c · vi

Potential Bugs & Security Vulnerabilities

A Potential Bug might crash your app tomorrow; a Security Vulnerability might let someone else break in today. SonarQube scans for both before deployment.

What is a Potential Bug?

  • A Potential Bug is a piece of code that may cause incorrect behavior, runtime exceptions, or unexpected results.
  • It is called "potential" because SonarQube predicts that the code could fail, even if it hasn't failed yet.
  • Potential Bug = Code that may behave incorrectly or crash in the future.

What is a Security Vulnerability?

  • A Security Vulnerability is a weakness in the code that an attacker could exploit to: Access unauthorized data · Modify information · Execute malicious actions · Compromise the application.
  • Security Vulnerability = A security weakness that attackers can exploit.

Why Do We Need to Detect Them?

⚠️ Banking Application — Bug Scenario
Money Transfer → Wrong Amount Calculated → Customers lose money.
⚠️ Banking Application — Vulnerability Scenario
Hacker → Steals Customer Data → The company may suffer financial and reputational damage.

That's why SonarQube checks both.

Why Does SonarQube Detect These?

ℹ️ Pattern Matching Against Rules
SonarQube scans your source code and compares it against predefined rules. It looks for patterns that commonly lead to: Runtime errors · Logical mistakes · Security attacks.

It warns developers before the application is deployed.

Example of a Potential Bug

Null Pointer Exception

Java
String name = null;
System.out.println(name.length());
⚠️ Problem
name is null. Calling .length() causes: NullPointerException. SonarQube warns you about this.

Example of a Security Vulnerability

SQL Injection

One of the most common interview questions.

Java — Bad
String query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + userInput;
⚠️ Risk
If the user enters malicious SQL, the query can be manipulated.
💡 Better
Use Prepared Statements or parameterized queries.

Real-Life Analogy

Potential Bug = A Crack in the Bridge
Imagine a bridge with a small crack. People may cross it today. But one day it may collapse. That crack is like a Potential Bug.
Security Vulnerability = An Unlocked Door
Imagine your house — the main door has no lock. Nothing has been stolen yet. But anyone can enter. That's a Security Vulnerability.

Enterprise Usage

🔖 CI/CD Integration
In companies like Cognizant, SonarQube runs during the CI/CD pipeline. If it detects Critical Bugs or Critical Security Vulnerabilities, the Quality Gate may fail.

Advantages of Detecting Them Early

Prevents application crashes Improves reliability Protects sensitive data Reduces production issues Saves debugging time Improves customer trust
Module 8 · Code Quality & SonarQube · 8c · vii

Insufficient Comments

Comments aren't about explaining every line — they're about explaining the lines that wouldn't otherwise explain themselves, six months from now, to you or someone else.

What are Comments?

  • Comments are notes written in the source code to help developers understand the purpose or logic of the code.
  • The compiler ignores comments — they are only for humans.

What is Insufficient Comments?

🔖 Not "Every Line," Just the Unclear Ones
Insufficient Comments means the code lacks necessary explanations where they would help developers understand complex logic.

It does not mean: "Every line must have a comment."
Instead: important or complex code should be explained when the code itself isn't clear enough.

Why Do We Need Comments?

You, Six Months Later
Imagine you wrote a project today. After 6 months, you open the same project. You see this:
Java
calculate();
process();
execute();

You may even ask yourself: "Why did I write this logic?"

Helps yourself (future maintenance) Helps other developers

Why Does SonarQube Check Comments?

⚠️ Large Enterprise Projects
Large enterprise projects may contain millions of lines of code, and new developers join regularly.

Without comments in important areas: Understanding business logic becomes difficult · Maintenance takes longer · Bugs are harder to fix.

So SonarQube encourages meaningful documentation.

When Should You Write Comments?

🧠

Complex Business Logic

Explain the "why," not just the "what"

🧮

Important Algorithms

Non-obvious calculations or logic

🩹

Workarounds

Explain why a hack was necessary

📡

Public APIs

Classes and methods used by other developers

When Should You Avoid Comments?

Avoid comments for code that is already obvious.

Java — Bad
// Increment i
i++;
💡 The Code Already Explains Itself
A comment restating what the code obviously does adds noise, not clarity.

Does SonarQube Check Comment Coverage?

  • Yes, SonarQube can check: Public classes without documentation · Public methods without JavaDoc (depending on configured rules) · Missing documentation in important code areas.
  • However, it does not require comments for every line.
  • The exact rules depend on the project's Quality Profile.

Advantages

Improves readability Helps new developers understand the code Simplifies maintenance Documents business rules Improves long-term maintainability

Reading a SonarQube Report — What to Fix First

A failed Quality Gate isn't a wall — it's a checklist. Knowing which metric to fix first turns a scary red report into a manageable to-do list.

What is a SonarQube Report?

  • A SonarQube Report is a summary of the code analysis performed by SonarQube.
  • It shows: Bugs · Security Vulnerabilities · Code Smells · Coverage · Duplicate Code · Cyclomatic Complexity · Quality Gate Status.
  • SonarQube Report = Health Report of your source code.

Reading a SonarQube Report

Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · i

Introduction to Microservices

A large, tangled monolith split into small, independent services — each owning one job, deployable on its own, scalable on its own, and unable to take the whole app down when it breaks.

What are Microservices?

  • Microservices is an architectural style where a large application is divided into multiple small, independent services, each performing one specific business function.
  • Each microservice: Has a single responsibility · Runs independently · Can be developed independently · Can be deployed independently · Communicates with other services through APIs or messages.

Real-Life Analogy

Building an Amazon-Like Application
Instead of creating one huge Spring Boot application containing Login, Product, Order, Payment, Delivery, and Notification...

you create separate Spring Boot applications: Login Service · Product Service · Order Service · Payment Service · Delivery Service · Notification Service

Each is called a Microservice. Together they behave like one application.

Why Do We Need Microservices?

Imagine an Online Shopping Website. Initially, 10 developers build this application — everything inside one project:

structure
Shopping Application
│
├── Login
├── Products
├── Orders
├── Payments
├── Delivery
├── Notification

Initially everything works fine. After 5 years: 100 developers · Millions of users · Hundreds of features. Problems begin.

⚠️ Problem 1 — Huge Project
One Project → 50 lakh lines of code.

Finding bugs becomes difficult · Understanding code becomes difficult · New developers need months to understand it.
⚠️ Problem 2 — Deployment Problem
Suppose you only change the Notification Module — you must still deploy the entire application.

Changed → Notification → Deploy Everything. Waste of time.
⚠️ Problem 3 — Scaling Problem
Suppose during Diwali, Search receives huge traffic — 500,000 requests — but Login receives only 1,000.

Still, the entire application must be scaled. Huge infrastructure cost.
⚠️ Problem 4 — One Bug Can Affect Everything
Suppose Payment crashes. Sometimes the whole application goes down because everything is tightly connected.
💡 Solution
Split the application — each feature becomes one independent service. That is Microservices.

Monolithic vs Microservices Architecture

Monolithic Architecture
                   Users
                     │
                     ▼
      +--------------------------------+
      |      One Spring Boot App       |
      |--------------------------------|
      | Login                          |
      | Product                        |
      | Order                          |
      | Payment                        |
      | Delivery                       |
      | Notification                   |
      +--------------------------------+
                     │
                     ▼
              One Database
Microservices Architecture
                     Users
                       │
                       ▼
                 API Gateway
      ┌──────────┼──────────┐
      ▼          ▼          ▼
 Login Service Product Service Order Service
                               │
                               ▼
                      Inventory Service
                               │
                               ▼
                      Payment Service
                               │
                               ▼
                   Notification Service

Each service usually has its own database.

Advantages

Business Advantages

Faster development Faster deployment Independent teams Easy maintenance Better scalability Fault isolation Easier technology upgrades Cloud-friendly architecture

Technical Advantages

Independent deployment Independent databases Better modularity Better CI/CD support Easier testing of individual services

Principles of Microservices

Four core principles keep microservices actually independent — one job per service, one database per service, independent deployments, and independent scaling.

Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

  • A Microservice should perform only one business function.
  • Each service should have one and only one responsibility.
⚠️ Why Do We Need SRP?
Imagine Amazon. Suppose Payment Service contains: Payment, Login, Notifications, Orders.

Now the Payment Team wants to update payment logic — they accidentally affect Login. Result: unexpected bugs.
With SRP: Payment Service
↓
Only Payment — no other functionality is affected

Decentralized Data Management

  • Each Microservice should own its own database.
  • No service should directly access another service's database.
⚠️ Why Do We Need It?
Imagine: Order Service ↓ Shared Database ↑ Payment Service.

Now Payment changes a table — Order Service breaks. Both become tightly coupled.
Order Service → Order Database
·
Payment Service → Payment Database

Each service manages its own data.

Different Bank Departments
Loan Department → Own records
Accounts Department → Own records
HR Department → Own records

Nobody edits another department's files directly.
Loose coupling Independent schema changes Better security Easier scaling Independent backups Better fault isolation

Continuous Delivery & Deployment (CD/CD)

  • Every microservice should be deployable independently.
  • A new version of one service should not require deploying the entire application.
🔖 Why Do We Need It?
Suppose only Notification changes.
🐘

Monolith

Deploy the entire application

⚡

Microservices

Deploy only the Notification Service — much faster

Mobile Apps
WhatsApp receives an update. Instagram does not. Each app updates independently.

Similarly, each Microservice is deployed independently.
Faster releases Less downtime Smaller deployments Easier rollback Lower deployment risk

Scalability & Flexibility

  • Each Microservice should scale independently based on demand.
🔖 Why Do We Need It?
Suppose Search receives 10 lakh requests, while Payment receives 1,000.
🐘

Monolith

Scale everything — waste of money

🎯

Microservices

Scale only the Search Service — very efficient

Better performance Lower infrastructure cost High availability Better cloud utilization Supports millions of users
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · iii

Challenges of Microservices

Independence isn't free — splitting one application into many buys you flexibility at the cost of new complexity, network calls, consistency puzzles, and visibility problems.

Complexity Management

  • Complexity Management means handling the increased complexity that arises when one application is split into many independent microservices.
🐘

Monolithic

One application — everything is in one place

🧩

Microservices

Login, Product, Order, Payment, Inventory, Notification, Review Service — many applications to manage

Instead of managing 1 application, you now manage many applications. This increases system complexity.

Shopping Mall
Managing one small shop is easy. Managing an entire shopping mall with 200 shops, security, electricity, parking, cleaning, and maintenance is much more complex.

Microservices are similar.
Better organization Independent teams Easier maintenance Faster development

Inter-Service Communication

  • Microservices communicate with each other using network calls instead of direct method calls.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need It?
Suppose Order Service needs payment confirmation. Order Service cannot directly call a Java method inside Payment Service because they are separate applications — instead, they communicate over the network.
Phone Call
Suppose you need information from another department. You don't walk into their computer — you call them, send an email, or send a message.

Microservices communicate similarly.
Network delay Timeout Service unavailable Retry failures Security Serialization issues

Data Consistency

  • Maintaining correct and synchronized data across multiple microservices is called Data Consistency.
  • Remember: each service has its own database.
⚠️ When Things Go Wrong Mid-Flow
Order Service → Order Database · Payment Service → Payment Database

Suppose: Order created successfully, but Payment failed.

Order Database says: Order Created. Payment Database says: Payment Failed.

The system becomes inconsistent.
Bank Transfer
Suppose ₹1000 leaves Account A. But the bank server crashes before adding ₹1000 to Account B — money disappears.

Banks solve this carefully. Microservices face similar challenges.
💡 Solutions (Studied Later)
Saga Pattern · Event Sourcing · CQRS — these patterns help maintain consistency.

Monitoring & Logging

  • Monitoring means tracking the health and performance of services.
  • Logging means recording events and errors generated by services.
⚠️ Why Do We Need It?
Suppose there are 50 Microservices, and one service fails. How will you know?

Without monitoring, users discover the problem before developers.

Monitoring tools collect information like:

CPU Usage Memory Usage Response Time Error Rate Availability
Hospital
Patients are connected to monitors. Doctors immediately know if something goes wrong.

Similarly, Monitoring tools continuously watch Microservices.
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · iv

Microservices Architecture Overview

A client never talks to individual services directly — a reception desk (API Gateway), a directory (Service Discovery), and a traffic cop (Load Balancer) sit in between, so no one has to hardcode an IP address.

Components of Microservices Architecture

  • A Microservices Architecture is a collection of components that work together to run multiple independent microservices as a single application.
Client (Browser/Mobile)
↓
API Gateway
↓
Service Discovery
↓
Microservices
↓
Databases

Additionally, in production we also have: Config Server · Monitoring · Logging · Security · Message Broker · Circuit Breaker — you'll study these later.

⚠️ Why Do We Need These Components?
Imagine Amazon has Login, Product, Order, Payment, Inventory, and Shipping services. Without any architecture, the client would need to know the IP address of every service:

Browser → Login → 192.168.1.20 → Order → 192.168.1.25 → Payment → 192.168.1.40

This is difficult to manage — instead, we introduce dedicated components.
Basic Microservices Architecture
               Users
                 │
      Mobile / Web Browser
                 │
                 ▼
          +----------------+
          |   API Gateway  |
          +----------------+
                 │
                 ▼
     +-------------------------+
     |   Service Discovery     |
     +-------------------------+
      │        │         │
      ▼        ▼         ▼
Login Service Product  Order Service
   │         Service        │
   ▼            │           ▼
Login DB      Product DB   Order DB
Office Reception
Visitors never directly enter different departments. They first go to the Reception Desk, which then directs them to HR, Finance, IT, or Sales.

Reception = API Gateway · Employee Directory = Service Discovery · Departments = Microservices

Service Discovery

  • Service Discovery is a mechanism that helps microservices find and communicate with each other automatically.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need It?
Suppose Order Service wants to call Payment Service. If Payment Service's IP changes — old 192.168.1.10 becomes new 192.168.1.25 — how will Order Service know?

Hardcoding IP addresses is not practical.
Payment Service
↓ Registers ↓
Service Discovery

Now Order Service asks: "Where is Payment Service?" Service Discovery replies: Payment Service → 192.168.1.25. No hardcoded IPs required.

Mobile Contacts
You don't remember everyone's phone number — you search the contact list.

Similarly, Microservices search Service Discovery instead of remembering IP addresses.

API Gateway

  • An API Gateway is the single entry point for all client requests. Clients never directly access microservices.
⚠️ Without an API Gateway
Client → Login Service → Product Service → Payment Service → Order Service

The client must know every service URL — difficult and insecure.
💡 With an API Gateway
Client → API Gateway → Required Service

Only one endpoint is exposed.
API Gateway Routing
         Client
            │
            ▼
    +----------------+
    |  API Gateway   |
    +----------------+
     │      │      │
     ▼      ▼      ▼
  Login  Product  Order
  Service Service Service

Responsibilities of API Gateway

Request Routing Authentication Authorization Rate Limiting SSL Termination Request Logging Load Balancing Response Aggregation

We'll study many of these later.

Airport Security
Passengers don't directly enter aircraft. Everyone first passes through Security, Verification, and the Gate.

Similarly, every request first passes through the API Gateway.

Load Balancing

  • Load Balancing distributes incoming requests among multiple instances of the same service.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need It?
Suppose Search Service receives 10 Lakh Requests. One server cannot handle all requests — instead, run multiple instances.
Load Balancing
             Users
               │
               ▼
        Load Balancer
      ┌──────┼──────┐
      ▼      ▼      ▼
 Search1 Search2 Search3

Instead of one server becoming overloaded, traffic is shared.

Common Algorithms

AlgorithmDescription
Round RobinRequests go one by one to each server
Least ConnectionsSend request to the least busy server
RandomRandom server selection
Weighted Round RobinPowerful servers receive more requests
Bank Counters
Customers arrive. The manager sends them to Counter 1, Counter 2, or Counter 3. No single counter becomes overloaded.

That's Load Balancing.

Advantages

High Availability Better Performance Fault Tolerance Horizontal Scalability Better User Experience
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · v

Microservices Design Patterns

Four patterns that solve the recurring problems of a distributed system — finding services, surviving failures, assembling responses, and keeping data consistent across independent databases.

Service Registry & Discovery Pattern

  • Allows microservices to register themselves and discover other services dynamically, without hardcoding IP addresses.
⚠️ Why Do We Need It?
Order Service needs to call Payment Service. Initially Payment Service runs on 192.168.1.20.

Later it is redeployed and moves to 192.168.1.45. If Order Service has the old IP stored, communication fails.

Hardcoding addresses is impossible in large systems.
Phone Contact List
You don't remember everyone's phone number — you search their name in your contacts.

Similarly, Microservices search the Service Registry.
No hardcoded IP addresses Dynamic discovery Easy scaling Easier deployments Fault tolerance

Circuit Breaker Pattern

  • Prevents repeated requests to a failed service — stops unnecessary network calls until the failed service recovers.
⚠️ Why Do We Need It?
Order Service calls Payment Service. Payment Service crashes.
Without Circuit Breaker
↓
Order → Payment → Retry → Payment → Retry → Payment → Retry...
↓
Thousands of useless requests overload the system
💡 Solution
The Circuit Breaker temporarily blocks requests.
Electrical Circuit Breaker
When there is an electrical fault, the breaker disconnects power to protect the system. After the fault is fixed, power is restored.

Microservices use the same idea.
Prevents cascading failures Improves availability Faster recovery Protects resources Better user experience

API Composition Pattern

  • Combines data from multiple microservices into one response.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need It?
Suppose the UI needs Customer Details, Order Details, and Payment Status — each belongs to a different service.
Without API Composition: UI
↓
Customer Service → Order Service → Payment Service
↓
Three network calls

Instead, the UI makes one request — the API Composer collects everything.

Restaurant Waiter
You order Pizza, Cold Drink, and Dessert. Different departments prepare them. The waiter brings everything together.

The waiter acts like an API Composer.
Fewer client requests Better performance Simpler frontend Reduced network traffic

Saga Pattern

  • Maintains data consistency across multiple microservices when each service has its own database.
⚠️ Why Do We Need It?
Remember: every service owns its own database. Suppose a customer buys a laptop.
Step 1 — Order Service: Order Created
↓
Step 2 — Payment Service: Payment Failed
↓
Now: Order exists, Payment doesn't — the system becomes inconsistent
💡 Solution
Saga coordinates multiple services. If one step fails, previous successful steps are compensated (rolled back logically).
Travel Booking
Booking a trip: Flight, Hotel, Payment. If one part fails, instead of keeping the flight and hotel bookings, everything is cancelled.

That's Saga.
Data consistency Distributed transactions Reliable workflows Failure recovery
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · vi

Inter-Service Communication

Because microservices are separate applications, they can't call each other's methods directly — they talk over the network, either waiting for a reply or firing and moving on, and they need a plan for when that network fails.

What is Inter-Service Communication?

  • Inter-Service Communication is the process by which one microservice communicates with another to complete a business operation.
  • Unlike a Monolithic application (where classes call each other directly), microservices are separate applications running on different servers or containers — so they communicate over a network.
🔖 Why Do We Need It?
Suppose a customer places an order. The Order Service cannot complete everything by itself — it needs help from Inventory Service, Payment Service, and Notification Service.
Order Service
↓
Inventory Service
↓
Payment Service
↓
Notification Service

Communication Types

Inter-Service Communication
↓
Synchronous · Asynchronous

Synchronous Communication

  • The sender sends a request and waits until the receiver responds.
TypeDescription
REST (Representational State Transfer)Uses HTTP and JSON. Easy to understand and widely used.
gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call)Uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers. Faster than REST, mainly used for internal communication.
Phone Call
You wait until the other person replies.
Immediate response Easy implementation Simple debugging REST is widely supported gRPC offers very high performance

Asynchronous Communication

  • The sender sends a message and continues its work without waiting for the receiver.
TypeExamplesBehavior
Message QueueRabbitMQ · ActiveMQUsually one consumer processes one message
Event StreamingApache Kafka · Apache PulsarOne event can be consumed by multiple services
Email
You send the email and continue your work. The receiver reads it later.
Better scalability Loose coupling Reliable communication Suitable for long-running tasks

Handling Failures & Retries

  • In distributed systems, network failures are common. Microservices must know how to recover safely.
Network timeout Service unavailable Slow response Server crash Database unavailable

Retry

Instead of failing immediately, retry the request.

Request
↓
Failed
↓
Retry
↓
Retry
↓
Success
🔖 Why Retry?
Sometimes failures are temporary. Example: Payment Service restarts, retry after 2 seconds — now it works.

Retry Strategies

StrategyBehavior
Fixed RetryEvery 2 seconds
Exponential BackoffRetry 1 → 1s · Retry 2 → 2s · Retry 3 → 4s · Retry 4 → 8s

Exponential Backoff is very common in production.

Fallback

💡 Fail Gracefully
Suppose Payment Service is unavailable. Instead of crashing, show: "Payment Service is temporarily unavailable. Please try again later."

Better user experience.

Circuit Breaker + Retry

Often used together.

Failure
↓
Retry
↓
Still Failed
↓
Circuit Breaker Opens
↓
Fallback Response
ATM
The ATM cannot contact the bank — it retries. If still unsuccessful, it shows: "Service Temporarily Unavailable" instead of crashing.

Advantages

Better reliability Better availability Better user experience Handles temporary failures
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · vii

Data Management

Every service owns its own database — and once you accept that, you also need ways to reconstruct history (Event Sourcing) and separate heavy reads from heavy writes (CQRS).

Database per Service

  • Each Microservice should have its own dedicated database.
  • No other microservice should directly read or write its database.
E-Commerce Application
Instead of one database, each service owns its own:
Order Service → Order Database
·
Payment Service → Payment Database
·
Inventory Service → Inventory Database
·
Notification Service → Notification Database

Each service controls its own data.

⚠️ Why Do We Need It?
Suppose all services share one database: Order Service → Payment Service → Inventory Service → Shared Database.

Problems: Tight coupling · One schema change affects everyone · Difficult deployment · Poor scalability · Security issues.

Event Sourcing

  • Instead of storing only the current state, store every event that happened.
  • The current state can always be recreated from those events.
🏦

Traditional Database

Bank account balance today: ₹7000. Only the current value is stored — you don't know how it became ₹7000.

📜

Event Sourcing

Store every event, so the current balance can always be calculated.

Account Created
↓
₹5000 Deposited
↓
₹2000 Deposited
↓
₹1000 Withdrawn
↓
₹1000 Deposited
🔖 Why Do We Need Event Sourcing?
Suppose a customer says "I lost ₹500." How will you investigate?

Traditional database — only the latest balance exists, impossible to trace history.
Event Sourcing — complete history is available.
Complete audit history Easy debugging Event replay Better analytics Supports Event-Driven Architecture
Complex implementation Large storage requirement Harder querying

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)

  • CQRS separates Write Operations and Read Operations into different models.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need CQRS?
Traditional application: One Database → Reads → Writes. Both operations use the same model.

Heavy read traffic slows writes. Heavy writes slow reads. CQRS separates them.
CQRS Diagram
             Client

        ┌────────────┐

        ▼            ▼

Command Model   Query Model

        │            │

        ▼            ▼

 Write Database  Read Database
ModelPurposeExamples
CommandChanges dataInsert · Update · Delete
QueryOnly reads dataSearch · Get Details · View Products
Better performance Better scalability Faster reads Independent optimization Easier maintenance
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · viii

Security

Who you are, what you're allowed to do, whether your data can be read in transit, and how you prove identity without handing over your password — four questions every microservice needs answered.

Authentication

  • Authentication is the process of verifying who the user is. It answers the question: "Who are you?"
🔖 Example
Suppose you log in to Amazon. You enter a Username and Password — the system checks whether these credentials are correct. If correct, you are authenticated.
Verifies user identity Prevents unauthorized access Protects user accounts Improves application security

Authorization

  • Authorization determines what an authenticated user is allowed to do. It answers the question: "What are you allowed to access?"
Controls permissions Protects sensitive data Prevents unauthorized actions Implements role-based access

Secure Communication (HTTPS)

  • HTTPS is a secure version of HTTP.
  • It encrypts data before sending it over the network.
⚠️ Why Do We Need HTTPS?
Suppose Login Service sends Username and Password using plain HTTP — anyone on the network can read it. Very dangerous.
Username / Password
↓
Encrypted
↓
Internet
↓
Decrypted

Nobody can read the data in transit.

Locked Courier Box
Suppose you send money — instead of sending it openly, you lock it inside a secure box. Only the receiver has the key.

HTTPS works similarly.
Data encryption Prevents data theft Prevents Man-in-the-Middle attacks Secure communication

OAuth2

  • OAuth2 is an authorization framework that allows users to grant applications limited access to their resources without sharing passwords.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need OAuth2?
Suppose you click "Login with Google." You never give your Google password to that application.

Instead: Google verifies you → Google sends an Access Token → the application trusts Google.
Hotel Reception
Instead of showing your house keys, you show your government ID. The hotel verifies your identity.

Similarly, OAuth2 lets another trusted service verify you.
Password never shared Secure login Supports Single Sign-On (SSO) Industry standard Easy integration with Google, GitHub, Facebook, Microsoft

Security Best Practices

🔒

1. Always Use HTTPS

Never expose APIs over plain HTTP

🚫

2. Never Hardcode Passwords

Use environment variables or a Config Server instead

✅

3. Validate Every Request

Never trust client input — always validate

🔑

4. Use Strong Passwords

Weak: 123456 · Strong: Xy@2026#Secure

🎯

5. Least Privilege Principle

Give only required permissions — never Admin access unnecessarily

🔄

6. Rotate Tokens

Access Tokens should expire — generate new ones regularly

🛡️

7. Encrypt Sensitive Data

Passwords · Credit Card Numbers · Personal Information

📋

8. Log Security Events

Login Success · Login Failure · Unauthorized Access · Token Expiration

⚠️ Never Do This
password = admin123
💡 Do This Instead
Read credentials from environment variables or a Config Server — never commit them to source code.

Introduction to Spring Cloud

Spring Boot builds one application. Spring Cloud manages the fact that you now have fifty of them — discovery, configuration, communication, and resilience, all standardized.

Spring Boot vs Spring Cloud

Spring BootSpring Cloud
Builds one applicationConnects multiple applications
Focus on application developmentFocus on distributed system management
StandaloneWorks with multiple services
Creates REST APIsManages communication, discovery, configuration, resilience

Introduction to Spring Cloud

  • Spring Cloud is a collection of tools and libraries that help developers build, manage, and deploy Microservices.
  • It provides solutions for common distributed system problems.

Why Do We Need Spring Cloud?

⚠️ Managing 50 Microservices Manually
Without Spring Cloud, you have to manually manage: Service locations · Configuration files · Communication · Fault handling · Load balancing.

This becomes extremely difficult. Spring Cloud automates these tasks.

Key Features of Spring Cloud

🔍

1. Service Discovery

Automatically detects and registers services. Example: Eureka Server.

🚪

2. API Gateway

Single entry point for all clients. Example: Spring Cloud Gateway.

⚙️

3. Configuration Management

Centralized configuration for all services. Example: Spring Cloud Config.

⚖️

4. Load Balancing

Distributes requests across multiple instances. Example: Ribbon.

🔌

5. Circuit Breaker

Prevents cascading failures. Example: Resilience4j or Hystrix.

🧵

6. Distributed Tracing

Tracks requests across services. Example: Zipkin.

🛡️

7. Security

Manages authentication and authorization. Example: Spring Security OAuth2.

☁️

8. Cloud Connectors

Integrates with cloud platforms. Example: Cloud Foundry Connector.

📊

9. Monitoring and Metrics

Provides insights into service performance. Example: Micrometer, Prometheus.

📡

10. Event-Driven Architecture

Enables asynchronous communication. Example: Spring Cloud Stream.

Benefits of Spring Cloud

Simplifies microservices development Enhances scalability and resilience Improves deployment flexibility Supports modern DevOps practices Reduces boilerplate code Facilitates integration with cloud platforms Provides standardized patterns for common issues

Common Spring Cloud Components

ComponentPurpose
EurekaService Discovery
Zuul / GatewayAPI Gateway
ConfigConfiguration Management
HystrixCircuit Breaker
OAuth2Security
StreamEvent-driven Messaging
GatewayRouting and Filtering
VaultSecret Management
Jenkins / GitLab CICI/CD Integration

Real-Life Analogy

Office Management
Employees can work individually. But to run the company smoothly, you also need Reception, HR, Security, and Administration.

Similarly, Spring Boot creates services. Spring Cloud manages them.

Centralized Configuration with Spring Cloud Config

Editing the same property across 20 services every time it changes doesn't scale — a single, centrally-managed configuration source does.

Configuring Microservices with Spring Cloud

  • Instead of storing configuration inside every service, Spring Cloud stores configuration centrally.

Why Do We Need It?

⚠️ 20 Services, Same Properties
Suppose 20 microservices have server.port, database.url, database.username, database.password.

If the database password changes, you must edit 20 applications. Very difficult.

Instead, Spring Cloud Config stores configuration in one place.

Real-Life Analogy

School Notice Board
Instead of informing every student individually, the principal updates one notice board. Everyone reads the same information.

Advantages

Centralized configuration Easy updates Better consistency Easier maintenance

Service Discovery & Registration using Netflix Eureka

Eureka is the Service Registry that turns "hardcode the IP and hope it never changes" into "ask the registry, every time."

What is Netflix Eureka?

  • Netflix Eureka is a Service Registry used by Spring Cloud.
  • It allows services to register themselves and discover other services automatically.

Why Do We Need Eureka?

⚠️ Payment Service Restarts
Old Address: 192.168.1.10 → New Address: 192.168.1.45

Without Eureka, other services fail.
With Eureka, Payment Service registers automatically — other services always get the latest location.

Advantages

Dynamic service discovery No hardcoded IPs Easy scaling Automatic registration High availability

Spring Security for Microservices

Being inside the network isn't the same as being allowed in — every microservice, even one talking only to trusted internal services, still authenticates and authorizes every request.

Overview of Spring Security

  • Spring Security is a powerful security framework provided by Spring that helps secure Spring Boot applications.
  • It provides: Authentication · Authorization · Password Encryption · Session Management · CSRF Protection · OAuth2 Support · JWT Integration.
⚠️ Why Do We Need Spring Security?
Suppose you create a REST API: GET /users · POST /payment · DELETE /products

Without security, anyone can access these APIs. Very dangerous. Spring Security protects these APIs.
Secure APIs Built-in Authentication Built-in Authorization Password Encryption OAuth2 Support Easy integration

Securing Microservices using Spring Security

  • Each microservice should protect its own APIs.
  • Even if services communicate internally, requests must still be authenticated and authorized.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need It?
Order Service → Payment Service. If Payment Service accepts every request, any attacker could send fake payment requests.

Spring Security verifies the request before processing it.
Bank Locker
Even inside the bank, you still need your locker key. Being inside the building doesn't automatically give access.

Similarly, one microservice must authenticate before accessing another.
Secure service communication Prevents fake requests Protects internal APIs Improves trust between services

Authentication & Authorization in a Microservices Environment

ConceptQuestionUsually Done Using
AuthenticationWho is making the request?Username & Password · JWT Token · OAuth2 Token
AuthorizationWhat resources can this user access?Roles & Permissions
🙋

Customer

View Products · Order Products

🛠️

Admin

Manage Products · Delete Users · View Reports

Airport
Passport Check → Authentication
Boarding Pass → Authorization
Role-based access Secure APIs Better control Protects sensitive data

Configuring Security for RESTful APIs

  • REST APIs should never be publicly accessible unless intentionally designed.
  • Spring Security secures REST endpoints.
⚠️ Why Do We Need It?
Suppose API: DELETE /users

Without security, anyone can delete users. Very dangerous.
Protects APIs Role-based access Prevents unauthorized requests Secure communication
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · xiii

Centralized Authentication

Logging in separately at every microservice would make Amazon unusable. One trusted Authentication Server, and a token every other service accepts, fixes that.

First, Understand the Problem

Suppose your company has 10 Microservices: Login Service · Order Service · Payment Service · Product Service · Customer Service.

Now imagine every service asks the user to login separately.

User
↓
Login Service (Login Required)
↓
Order Service (Login Again)
↓
Payment Service (Login Again)
↓
Inventory Service (Login Again)
↓
Notification Service (Login Again)
⚠️ Imagine Using Amazon Like This
Open Orders → Login · Open Payment → Login · Open Cart → Login · Open Profile → Login

Impossible.

Why Do We Need Centralized Authentication?

Instead of every service authenticating users, we create one central authentication system.

User
↓
Authentication Server
↓
User Verified
↓
Access Token Issued
↓
Order Service · Payment Service · Inventory Service

User logs in only once. All services trust the Authentication Server.

What is Centralized Authentication?

🔖 Definition
Centralized Authentication means only one server is responsible for verifying the identity of every user. All Microservices trust this server.

Advantages

Single Login Better Security Easy User Management Easy Password Change No Duplicate Login Logic Better Scalability Centralized User Database Easier Maintenance

Disadvantages

⚠️ Single Point of Failure
The Authentication Server becomes critical — if it goes down, users cannot login.

Therefore, companies deploy multiple Authentication Servers for high availability.
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · xiv

OAuth 2.1 & OpenID Connect (OIDC)

OAuth2 answers "does this request have permission?" OIDC answers "who exactly is making it?" — two different questions, often asked together.

ℹ️ One-Line Distinction
OAuth2 provides Authorization. OIDC provides Authentication.

OAuth 2.1

  • OAuth2 is an Authorization Framework that allows one application to access another application's resources without sharing the user's password.
Login with Google
Suppose you want to login into a shopping app using Google. Instead of giving your Google password to the shopping app, you login directly on Google's website.

Google verifies you and sends a token. The shopping app trusts Google. Your password is never shared.
⚠️ Why Do We Need OAuth2?
Imagine this dangerous situation:

Shopping App → "Please Enter Google Password Here"

Very risky. If the app is hacked, your Google account is compromised. OAuth2 solves this problem.
Password never shared Secure login Industry standard Supports third-party login Easy integration

OpenID Connect (OIDC)

  • It is an Identity Layer built on top of OAuth2.
  • It adds Authentication on top of Authorization.
  • OIDC tells the application: Who the user is.
🔖 OAuth2 vs OIDC — What Each One Tells You
OAuth2 only says: User has permission.

OIDC additionally says: User is Vishal. Email: abc@gmail.com. Verified User.

Identity information comes from OIDC.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need OIDC?
Suppose an application receives an Access Token — great. But who owns this token? OAuth2 doesn't tell us. OIDC solves this.
User identity Secure login Standard authentication Works with OAuth2 Supports SSO

Access Token vs ID Token

Access TokenID Token
Used to access APIsUsed to identify the user
OAuth2OIDC
PermissionIdentity
Resource AccessUser Information
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · xv

Authorization Server & Resource Server

One server creates the tokens, another server checks them. Splitting those two jobs is what lets a single login work safely across every microservice.

🔖 Two Questions, Two Servers
We know: OAuth2 gives an Access Token, OIDC gives an ID Token.

Who creates these tokens? → The Authorization Server
Who checks whether these tokens are valid? → The Resource Server

Authorization Server

  • The Authorization Server is responsible for: Authenticating users · Verifying credentials · Generating Tokens · Issuing Tokens.
  • It is the "Login Server" of the system.
Logging in with Google
Google checks your Username and Password. If everything is correct, Google generates an Access Token and an ID Token.

Google acts as the Authorization Server.
⚠️ Why Do We Need an Authorization Server?
Without it, every microservice would need to store users, verify passwords, and generate tokens — this creates duplicate work.

Instead, one server handles authentication for everyone.

Responsibilities

User Authentication Token Generation Token Expiration Refresh Tokens User Identity

Advantages

Centralized authentication Secure login Easy user management Standard OAuth2 implementation Supports SSO

Resource Server

  • The Resource Server hosts protected APIs.
  • It validates incoming tokens before allowing access.
ℹ️ Example
Suppose Payment Service has POST /payment. Only authenticated users should access it.

Payment Service checks the Access Token. If valid, the request is processed. Otherwise, the request is rejected.

Responsibilities

Protects APIs Validates JWT Checks Expiration Checks User Roles Grants or Denies Access

Advantages

Protects APIs Secure communication Easy access control

Authorization Server vs Resource Server

Authorization ServerResource Server
Authenticates UserValidates Token
Creates TokensChecks Tokens
Issues JWTReads JWT
LoginAPI Access
Stores UsersProtects APIs
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · xvi

JSON Web Token (JWT)

Log in once, get a JWT, and use it everywhere else — no username and password sent on every single request, and no server-side session to keep track of.

What is JWT?

  • JWT (JSON Web Token) is a secure token used to exchange user information between systems.
  • It proves that: User is authenticated · User is authorized — without sending the username and password every time.
🔖 How It's Used
Normally, you login once. After login, the server gives you a JWT.

Whenever you access another API, you send only the JWT — you do not send your username and password again.
No repeated login Stateless Authentication Faster API requests Easy to scale Perfect for Microservices

Structure of JWT

  • JWT has three parts: Header.Payload.Signature
JWT
xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz

The dot (.) separates each part.

How It Works

User logs in successfully
↓
Server generates a JWT and sends it to the client
↓
Client stores the JWT
↓
Client includes the JWT in the Authorization header on every request
↓
Server validates the JWT on each request

Header

Stores information about the token.

JSON
{
  "alg":"HS256",
  "typ":"JWT"
}
FieldDescription
algEncryption/Signing algorithm
typToken Type (JWT)
💡 Memory Trick
Header → How the JWT is protected.

Payload

Stores user information.

JSON
{
  "username":"Vishal",
  "role":"ADMIN",
  "email":"abc@gmail.com"
}

These values are called Claims.

Types of Claims

📋

a) Registered Claims

Standard fields — sub, iss, exp, aud

🌐

b) Public Claims

Application-specific — role, department

🔐

c) Private Claims

Custom values — college, employeeId, branch

Signature

  • The Signature protects the JWT.
  • If anyone changes the Payload, the Signature becomes invalid — the request is rejected.
Principal's Signature
Anyone can write a certificate. But only the Principal's signature proves it is genuine.

A JWT signature works the same way.

Access Token vs Refresh Token

Access TokenRefresh Token
Short LifeLong Life
Access APIsGenerate New Access Token
Sent with Every RequestUsed Occasionally
Expires QuicklyExpires Later

JWT vs Session Authentication

JWTSession
StatelessStateful
Server stores nothingServer stores Session
Better ScalabilityLimited Scalability
Best for APIsBest for Traditional Web Apps
Ideal for MicroservicesBetter for Monolithic Apps
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · xvii

Single Sign-On (SSO)

Login to Gmail once, and YouTube, Drive, Photos, Maps, and Calendar all just work — that's SSO, and it's the practical payoff of Centralized Authentication, OAuth2, OIDC, and JWT working together.

Before We Start

Suppose you use Google. You first open Gmail — login required, you login.

Now you open: YouTube · Google Drive · Google Photos · Google Maps · Google Calendar

💡 Do You Login Again?
No. Because Google uses Single Sign-On (SSO).

What is Single Sign-On?

  • Single Sign-On (SSO) is an authentication mechanism that allows a user to login once and access multiple applications without logging in again.
  • Instead of remembering and entering passwords for every application, you login only once.
  • That login is trusted by all applications.
One Login Better User Experience Faster Access Fewer Passwords Better Security Centralized Authentication Easier User Management

Where is SSO Used?

Almost everywhere.

Google Microsoft Facebook GitHub Amazon AWS Azure Portal Salesforce Jira Slack Enterprise Employee Portals

Technologies Used for SSO

OAuth2 OpenID Connect (OIDC) JWT SAML Keycloak Okta Auth0 Azure Active Directory

SSO vs Normal Login

Normal LoginSingle Sign-On
Login for every applicationOne login for all applications
Multiple passwordsOne authentication
Poor user experienceBetter user experience
Hard to manageEasy centralized management

Microservices Communication with Spring Cloud

OpenFeign turns a network call into a Java interface call. Orchestration and Choreography are the two opposite ways to coordinate that call across several services.

Inter-Service Communication Patterns

  • An Inter-Service Communication Pattern defines how microservices exchange information to complete a business process.
🔖 Why Do We Need It?
Imagine an E-Commerce application. A customer places an order — the Order Service cannot complete everything alone.

It needs to communicate with: Inventory Service · Payment Service · Notification Service.
TypeBehaviorExamples
SynchronousWaits for responseREST · gRPC
AsynchronousDoesn't waitKafka · RabbitMQ
Business collaboration Independent services Better scalability Distributed architecture

Spring Cloud OpenFeign

  • OpenFeign is a Declarative REST Client provided by Spring Cloud.
  • It allows one microservice to call another without writing manual HTTP client code.
ℹ️ What Does "Declarative" Mean?
Normally, to call another service, developers write lots of HTTP client code.

With OpenFeign, we simply declare an interface — Spring generates the implementation automatically.
Java
@FeignClient(name = "payment-service")
public interface PaymentClient {
    @GetMapping("/payment/{id}")
    Payment getPayment(@PathVariable Long id);
}
NameDescriptionPurposeExample
@FeignClientDeclares Feign ClientCalls another Microservice@FeignClient(name="payment-service")
nameService Name in EurekaFinds Servicepayment-service
@GetMappingHTTP GETFetch Data@GetMapping("/payment/{id}")
@PathVariableReads URL ValuePasses ParameterLong id
Personal Assistant
Instead of calling someone yourself, you tell your assistant: "Please contact the Payment Department." The assistant handles everything.

OpenFeign works exactly like that assistant.
Less code Automatic REST calls Integrates with Eureka Better readability Easy maintenance

Service Orchestration

  • In Orchestration, one central service controls the complete workflow.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need It?
Suppose a customer places an order. One service decides: Reserve Inventory · Process Payment · Send Notification.

Everything is centrally controlled.
Centralized control Easier debugging Predictable workflow
Single Point of Failure Tight coupling

Service Choreography

  • In Choreography, there is no central controller.
  • Every service reacts independently to events.
Loose coupling Better scalability Independent services
Hard debugging Difficult monitoring Complex event flow

Orchestration vs Choreography

OrchestrationChoreography
Central ControllerNo Controller
Easy MonitoringHard Monitoring
Tight CouplingLoose Coupling
Easier DebuggingDifficult Debugging
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · xix

API Gateway and Edge Services

The Gateway is traffic police for your microservices — it routes, filters, load-balances, and keeps the system alive even when a service behind it fails.

What is an API Gateway?

  • An API Gateway is the single entry point for all client requests in a Microservices Architecture.
  • It receives every client request and forwards it to the correct microservice.

Instead of the client directly calling different services, the client sends every request to the API Gateway. The API Gateway decides which service should receive the request.

Single Entry Point Better Security Request Routing Centralized Authentication Load Balancing

Spring Cloud Gateway

  • Spring Cloud Gateway is the official API Gateway provided by Spring Cloud.
  • It performs: Routing · Filtering · Authentication · Rate Limiting · Load Balancing · Logging.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need Spring Cloud Gateway?
Instead of writing routing logic manually, Spring Cloud Gateway automatically manages request routing.
Traffic Police
Traffic Police directs vehicles to different roads.

Similarly, Spring Cloud Gateway directs requests to different services.
Easy Routing Built-in Filters Eureka Integration Better Performance Centralized Security

Edge Services

  • Edge Services are services that interact directly with external clients.
  • An API Gateway is the most common Edge Service.

Routing

  • Routing means forwarding a request to the correct microservice.
/products
↓
Product Service
/orders
↓
Order Service

Filtering

  • Filtering means processing a request before or after routing.
➡️

Pre-Filters

Process request before routing — Authentication · Logging · Token Validation

⬅️

Post-Filters

Process response after routing — Response Logging · Header Modification · Compression

Airport Security
Before boarding, security checks your passport. After landing, immigration checks documents.

Similarly, Gateway filters process requests before and after routing.
Cleaner architecture Better security Centralized logging Easy monitoring

Load Balancing in API Gateway

  • Load Balancing distributes requests among multiple service instances.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need It?
Suppose Payment Service has three instances: Payment-1 · Payment-2 · Payment-3.

Instead of sending every request to Payment-1, the Gateway distributes them.
Better Performance High Availability Better Scalability Prevents Overloading

Resilience Patterns in API Gateway

  • Resilience Patterns keep the system running even when some services fail.
PatternDescription
Circuit BreakerStops repeated failures
RetryRetries temporary failures
TimeoutSets time limits — stops waiting after a certain time
FallbackProvides alternative response
Hospital Emergency Plan
If one doctor is unavailable, another doctor handles the patient. The hospital continues working.
High Availability Better Reliability Better User Experience Prevents Cascading Failures
Module 9 · Microservices & Spring Cloud · 9a · xx

Fault Tolerance and Resilience

An aircraft keeps flying on one engine — that's fault tolerance. A person recovers from a setback and moves forward — that's resilience. Microservices need both.

What is Fault Tolerance?

  • Fault Tolerance is the ability of a system to continue working even when some components fail.
🔖 Example
Suppose Payment Service crashes. Instead of crashing the whole application, the system continues operating using alternative strategies.
Aircraft
Even if one engine fails, the aircraft can continue flying safely.

This is Fault Tolerance.
High Availability Better User Experience Prevents System Failure Business Continuity

What is Resilience?

  • Resilience is the ability of a system to adapt and recover quickly from failures.
  • It's like bouncing back from a setback.
Person
When a person faces a challenge: they adapt, they recover, they move forward.

That's Resilience.
Quick Recovery Adaptability Reduced Downtime Improved Stability

Fault Tolerance vs Resilience

Fault Tolerance → Keeps system running
·
Resilience → Helps system recover quickly

Spring Cloud Hystrix

  • Hystrix was a Netflix library used to implement: Circuit Breaker · Fallback · Fault Tolerance.
Electrical Fuse
When overload occurs, the fuse disconnects electricity, protecting the system.
Prevents Cascading Failures Supports Fallback Better Stability

Circuit Breaker

  • Circuit Breaker prevents repeated requests to a failed service.

Fallback Mechanism

  • Fallback provides an alternative response when the main service is unavailable.
💡 Example
Payment Service crashes. Instead of a 500 Internal Server Error, the user sees: "Payment Service is temporarily unavailable. Please try again later."

The application still responds gracefully.
Backup Generator
When main power fails, the backup generator kicks in — it ensures continuity.
Improved User Experience System Stability Graceful Degradation

Retry Strategy

  • Retry automatically retries a failed request before giving up.
🔖 Why?
Sometimes failures are temporary. Example: Network timeout — second attempt succeeds.
Phone Call
Call → Busy → Try Again → Busy → Try Again → Connected.
Handles Temporary Failures Better Reliability Automatic Recovery

Handling Transient Faults

  • A Transient Fault is a temporary failure that disappears after some time.
Network Timeout Temporary Database Failure Temporary Service Unavailable High Network Latency
💡 Solution
Use: Retry · Circuit Breaker · Timeout · Fallback

Spring Cloud Config

One Config Server, stored in Git, feeding every microservice — change a property once, refresh without restarting, and let dev/test/prod each keep their own settings.

What is Externalized Configuration?

  • Externalizing configuration means storing configuration details outside the application code.
  • Instead of storing configuration inside every microservice, we keep it in one central location.

Why? Flexibility · Environment-specific settings · Security (secrets not in code).

⚠️ Without Externalized Configuration
Order Service → application.properties · Payment Service → application.properties · Inventory Service → application.properties

Every project stores its own configuration. Changing one property means changing every project.
Config Server (application.properties)
↓
Order Service · Payment Service · Inventory Service

Only one place to manage configuration.

Car Settings
Instead of hardcoding seat position and mirror angle in car design, these are adjustable externally.
Easy Updates Environment Flexibility Security Reusability

Spring Cloud Config

  • Spring Cloud Config provides a central Config Server that stores configuration for all Microservices.

Where does the Config Server store configurations? Usually: Git Repository · Local Files · File System · Vault · Database.

Most companies use Git.

🔖 Why Git?
Because Git provides: Version Control · History · Rollback · Team Collaboration.
Google Drive
Instead of everyone storing files separately, everyone downloads the latest file from Google Drive.

Config Server behaves similarly.
Central Management Git Integration Version Control Easy Deployment Better Consistency

Dynamic Configuration Updates

Without Dynamic Refresh: Restart Application. Very bad.

Monitoring and Metrics in Microservices

Actuator exposes the numbers, Prometheus collects and stores them, Grafana turns them into dashboards you can actually read at a glance.

Introduction to Microservices Monitoring

  • Monitoring is the process of continuously checking the health and performance of Microservices.
  • It helps detect issues before users do.
🚫

Without Monitoring

Payment Service → Slow → Nobody Knows. Users complain first.

✅

With Monitoring

Payment Service → CPU High → Alert Generated → Engineer Fixes Problem

Hospital ICU
Doctors continuously monitor Heart Rate, Oxygen, and Blood Pressure.

Similarly, Microservices are continuously monitored.
Detect failures early Better performance High Availability Faster debugging

Spring Boot Actuator

  • Spring Boot Actuator provides production-ready endpoints to monitor a Spring Boot application.
  • It gives insights into the application's internals.
⚠️ Without Actuator
Developers manually collect Memory, Health, CPU, and Threads — very difficult.
💡 With Actuator
Everything is available through endpoints.

Prometheus

  • Prometheus is a powerful monitoring and alerting toolkit.
  • It collects metrics from applications and stores them in a time-series database.
  • It is widely used in microservices architectures.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need Prometheus?
Actuator provides metrics. But — who stores them? Prometheus.

How does Prometheus work? Prometheus periodically pulls (scrapes) metrics from applications — it does not wait for applications to send them.

Attendance Teacher
Instead of students reporting attendance, the teacher checks attendance periodically.

Prometheus works the same way.
Time-Series Database Automatic Metric Collection Fast Queries Open Source

Grafana

  • Grafana is a visualization tool that works with Prometheus.
  • It displays metrics collected by Prometheus in beautiful dashboards.
  • It helps understand system behavior easily.
ℹ️ Why Do We Need Grafana?
Prometheus stores data. But — how do we see it? Grafana = Visualizer.
Data in Excel vs Data in Graphs
Grafana = Graphs.
Beautiful Dashboards Multiple Data Sources Real-Time Updates Easy to Use

Application Metrics

  • Application Metrics measure the health and performance of the application itself.
Request Count Response Time Error Rate Active Sessions Thread Count Database Connections
Factory
Factory Manager tracks Production, Defects, and Working Machines.

Similarly, developers monitor applications.
Performance Analysis Capacity Planning Faster Debugging

System Metrics

  • System Metrics measure the health and performance of the underlying system.
CPU Usage Memory Usage Disk I/O Network I/O Load Average
Hospital
Doctors check Heart Rate, Temperature, and Blood Pressure.

Similarly, system metrics check CPU, Memory, and Disk.
Resource Management Performance Tuning Predictive Maintenance

Security Best Practices in Microservices

Bank security isn't just a vault — it's CCTV, guards, passwords, and alarms together. Microservices security works the same way: many layers, not one.

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

  • RBAC is a security model where permissions are assigned to roles, and users receive permissions through their assigned role.
🚫

Without RBAC

Every user can access everything. Very dangerous.

✅

With RBAC

Admin: Manage Users, Delete Products, View Reports. Customer: View Products, Place Orders.

Airport Security
Different access levels based on roles: Security personnel → Full access. Passengers → Limited access.
Centralized Control Easy Management Reduced Errors Compliance

Securing Communication Between Microservices

  • Securing communication between services is crucial to prevent unauthorized access and data breaches.
⚠️ Consider a Banking Application
User Service · Account Service · Transaction Service

If not secured: Any service could access sensitive data · Data breaches occur · Financial loss.

How to Secure Communication?

Use HTTPS for all internal communications Implement service-to-service authentication Use API Gateways with built-in security features Employ mutual TLS (mTLS) for encrypted communication

Best Practices

HTTPS Everywhere Validate JWT Use Mutual TLS (mTLS) for internal communication Never expose internal services directly
Corporate Network
Employees can access internal systems. External parties cannot. Firewalls and access controls enforce this.
Data Protection Prevents Unauthorized Access Ensures Integrity Compliance with Regulations

Securing Sensitive Data

  • Securing sensitive data involves protecting information from unauthorized access, disclosure, or theft.

What is Sensitive Data?

Passwords API Keys Database Passwords Credit Card Numbers JWT Secrets OAuth Client Secrets
⚠️ Why Is It Important?
Data Breaches → Financial Loss · Legal Consequences · Reputational Damage

Regulatory Compliance → GDPR · HIPAA · PCI DSS

How to Secure Sensitive Data?

🔐

Encryption

At Rest · In Transit

🎯

Access Control

RBAC · ABAC

🎭

Data Masking

Hide sensitive details in logs or displays

🔍

Regular Audits

Monitor access · Identify vulnerabilities

Best Practices

Encrypt All Sensitive Data Use Strong Encryption Algorithms Implement Key Management Regular Security Assessments Data Loss Prevention (DLP) Tools
Safe in a Bank
Only authorized personnel can access. Multiple layers of security.
Privacy Protection Compliance Risk Mitigation Trust Building

Security Policies & Best Practices

PracticeDescription
AuthenticationAlways verify user identity
AuthorizationGrant only required permissions
Least PrivilegeGive users only the permissions they need
HTTPS EverywhereEncrypt all communication
Validate JWTNever trust incoming tokens blindly
Token ExpirationAlways configure token expiry
Input ValidationPrevent SQL Injection, XSS, and invalid inputs
LoggingLog security events — never log Passwords, JWT Tokens, or Credit Card Numbers
MonitoringMonitor Failed Login Attempts, Suspicious Requests, Unauthorized Access
Regular UpdatesKeep Spring Boot, Spring Security, and Dependencies up to date
Bank Security
Bank Security includes CCTV, Security Guards, Password, Vault, and Alarm — not just one security layer.

Similarly, Microservices use multiple security layers.
Strong Security Better Compliance Prevents Data Leaks Protects Business
